findings.title: Out-of-bounds read in serialized string ('S') unescaping (unserialize_str)
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/var_unserializer.re — unserialize_str(), reached from the 'S' (escaped binary string) grammar rule
findings.mechanism: unserialize_str() walks the serialized payload copying `len` logical characters while bounding reads against `end = *p + maxlen`. For each output character it checks `if (*p >= end) return NULL` ONCE per outer iteration. However, when the current byte is a backslash escape ('\\'), it enters an inner loop that executes `(*p)++` and then dereferences `**p` twice (to read two hex digits) WITHOUT re-checking `*p` against `end`. If a backslash appears as (or near) the last byte of the bounded region, the pointer is advanced to or past `end` and `**p` is dereferenced beyond the intended string extent. The outer per-character bounds check does not protect the two in-loop advances, so an attacker who crafts an 'S' token whose escape sequence is truncated at the buffer boundary can cause the parser to read 1–2 bytes past the region it was told to stay within. Depending on how the terminating/limit pointer is derived for the token, this is an over-read of the serialized buffer, and the decoded (attacker-influenced) byte is then stored into the freshly allocated zend_string, giving an information-leak primitive.
findings.reachable_how: Reachable by any application that calls unserialize() (directly or indirectly) on untrusted input — a ubiquitous pattern for PHP session payloads, cookies, cache blobs, and queue messages that a remote, unauthenticated client controls. The 'S' rule is part of the standard serialization grammar, so no special configuration is required; a malicious serialized string with a backslash escape placed at the end of the declared length triggers the unchecked inner reads.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled length/offset handling in binary request parsers (defense-in-depth concern)
findings.subsystem: main/fastcgi.c (fcgi_get_params / fcgi_read_request) and main/rfc1867.c (multipart_buffer_read / read_body)
findings.mechanism: These are the first code to touch raw, unauthenticated request bytes. fcgi_get_params() decodes 1- or 4-byte name/value length prefixes and validates `name_len + val_len > (end - p)` using unsigned arithmetic; the bounds logic is correct for the current masking (max 0x7fffffff each, no 32-bit wrap), but it is the canonical location where a single sign/masking regression would convert directly into a heap over-read because the subsequent fcgi_hash_set() copies `name_len`/`val_len` bytes straight out of a fixed `buf[FCGI_MAX_LENGTH+8]`. Likewise rfc1867's multipart boundary/length math (`len = max < bytes-1 ? max : bytes-1`, buffer refill bookkeeping) is fed entirely by attacker POST data. I did not find an exploitable flaw in the committed form, but these are the highest-value remote-reachable surfaces and any off-by-one in their length validation is immediately memory-unsafe.
findings.reachable_how: fastcgi params are parsed on every request handled by php-fpm/FastCGI; rfc1867 multipart parsing runs for any multipart/form-data POST. Both execute before any application-level authentication, so a completely unauthenticated remote client reaches them with fully controlled bytes.

t618.why: The finding is an unserialize 'S' escape over-read. It does not involve an OOM during request startup, multipart parsing, or cleanup of partially-initialized state.

t619.why: The finding does not involve stale per-request global state surviving a fatal error, nor a use-after-free on a reused worker via session upload progress.

t618.why: Touches the multipart parsing subsystem but covers length/bounds math, not an OOM during startup followed by cleanup of partially-initialized request state.

findings.title: Unserialize string-length boundary handling (primary remote-reachable memory-safety sink)
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/var_unserializer.re (php_var_unserialize)
findings.mechanism: The 's:'/'S:'/object-property string paths read an attacker-declared length via parse_uiv() and then validate it against the remaining buffer with `maxlen = max - YYCURSOR; if (maxlen < len) error`. After `YYCURSOR += len` the code dereferences YYCURSOR and YYCURSOR+1 to check the trailing '"' and ';'. Correctness depends entirely on (a) the declared length being rejected when it exceeds the remaining bytes and (b) the input buffer being NUL-terminated so that the one/two trailing dereferences after a maximal length stay in-bounds. Any weakening of the `maxlen < len` comparison (e.g. to `<=`), of the IS_FAKE_ELEM_COUNT element-count sanity checks, or of the NUL-termination guarantee turns this into an out-of-bounds read/write because `len` bytes are then copied (unserialize_str) or aliased (plain 's:') past the allocation. In the version I read these checks are present and consistent with upstream, but this is the canonical class of defect for this subsystem and the first place to verify byte-for-byte.
findings.reachable_how: unserialize() is routinely invoked on attacker-controlled data in real deployments (PHP session payloads, cached blobs, cookies, API bodies), so a remote unauthenticated client controls the serialized stream reaching this parser without any privileged step.

findings.title: FastCGI FCGI_PARAMS name/value length decoding
findings.subsystem: main/fastcgi.c (fcgi_get_params / fcgi_read_request)
findings.mechanism: Variable name/value lengths are decoded from the wire as up to 31-bit big-endian quantities and bounds-checked with `name_len + val_len > (unsigned int)(end - p)`. Each record is capped to FCGI_MAX_LENGTH (0xffff) and both lengths are capped to 0x7fffffff, so the unsigned addition cannot wrap past 2^32 and the check holds in the code as written. This is nonetheless the classic overflow-prone spot: if either the per-record length cap or the masking of the high byte were altered, the additive bounds check could wrap and permit fcgi_hash_set() to read far past the stack buffer `buf[FCGI_MAX_LENGTH+8]`. I verified the guards are intact here.
findings.reachable_how: Reachable by whatever can open the FastCGI socket (php-fpm). In misconfigurations where the FPM port is exposed, this is remote and unauthenticated; otherwise it is reached from the fronting web server translating untrusted request headers into FCGI_PARAMS.

findings.title: CLI built-in server request body/header assembly
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c (on_body, cli_concat_persistent_zstr_with_char, on_query_string)
findings.mechanism: Request body bytes are accumulated by first allocating `pemalloc(parser->content_length, 1)` and then growing with `perealloc(content, content_len + length)` before each memmove; header/query assembly similarly reallocs to the running length + new length and relies on ZEND_ASSERT bounds relative to PHP_HTTP_MAX_HEADER_SIZE. These are safe as written because capacity is re-established to the exact running total before every copy, but the correctness hinges on the reallocation always using the post-append size and on the header-size assertions being compiled in. If any of those size expressions were reduced (e.g. omitting the `+ length` growth, or trusting content_length as the final capacity), the subsequent memmove would overflow the heap buffer with directly attacker-controlled bytes.
findings.reachable_how: The built-in web server parses raw HTTP requests from any client; when exposed it is fully remote and unauthenticated, and these callbacks run on every request line, header, and body chunk before any user PHP executes.

findings.title: Unbounded stack copy of peer address into fixed 64-byte buffer during $_SERVER setup (built-in server)
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c, sapi_cli_server_register_variables() (REMOTE_ADDR/REMOTE_PORT registration)
findings.mechanism: When populating the per-request server variables, the code locates the last ':' in the connection's textual peer address (client->addr_str), computes addr_len = addr_end - addr_start (the substring before the port), and then does strncpy(addr, addr_start, addr_len) into a fixed-size stack buffer declared as 'char addr[64]', followed by addr[addr_len] = '\0'. There is no check that addr_len < sizeof(addr). strncpy copies exactly addr_len bytes with no NUL guarantee, and the explicit terminator write at addr[addr_len] lands past the end of the 64-byte buffer whenever the address portion is 64 bytes or longer. Both the bulk copy and the terminator write are therefore out-of-bounds stack writes if the formatted address string ever exceeds the buffer. The adjacent 'char port[8]' is handled with strncpy+forced terminator and is size-safe, but 'addr' is not bounds-checked at all. The ZEND_ASSERT(addr_len == strlen(addr)) that follows is compiled out in release builds and does nothing to prevent the overflow.
findings.reachable_how: Reached on every HTTP request handled by the PHP built-in development server (php -S) during request state set-up: sapi_activate -> register_variables -> sapi_cli_server_register_variables runs before user script code to build $_SERVER. The destination contents come from the accepted socket's formatted peer address; the branch is taken whenever that string contains a ':'. The dangerous aspect is a fixed stack buffer filled from a runtime-length string with no bound against the destination size, so any code path that yields an address representation of 64+ bytes produces an out-of-bounds stack write during normal request initialization.

findings.title: FastCGI name/value length parsing relies solely on a single comparison with no explicit overflow/termination guarantees
findings.subsystem: main/fastcgi.c, fcgi_get_params() (FCGI_PARAMS / FCGI_GET_VALUES decoding)
findings.mechanism: The parameter decoder reads attacker-supplied 1- or 4-byte length prefixes into unsigned int name_len/val_len (each up to 0x7fffffff), then validates with a single bound check 'name_len + val_len > (end - p)' before calling fcgi_hash_set(p, name_len, p+name_len, val_len). The safety of the subsequent reads of name_len and val_len bytes from the buffer depends entirely on that one comparison; the 4-byte-length branches only verify 'p + 3 >= end' before consuming the length bytes, and the computation/consumption 'p += name_len + val_len' assumes the single check fully constrains both fields. Any arithmetic edge (and the general fragility of trusting a client-provided length that is only loosely tied to the record content length FCGI_MAX_LENGTH) makes this a place where an out-of-bounds read into the hash store is a realistic failure mode.
findings.reachable_how: Reached when PHP runs as FastCGI/php-fpm and a client speaks the FastCGI protocol to the listening socket (notably when the fpm/cgi socket is exposed over TCP, a common misconfiguration). fcgi_read_request -> fcgi_get_params is executed during request set-up to populate the environment/params hash before any script runs, so the bytes feeding name_len/val_len are directly under the connecting party's control.

findings.title: Use-after-free / double-free of request header strings in the built-in web server (shared heap object without reference counting)
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — HTTP request header parsing and request-state lifecycle (php_cli_server_client_save_header, php_cli_server_request_ctor/dtor, apache_request_headers)
findings.mechanism: Each parsed header value is a single heap-allocated zend_string. In php_cli_server_client_save_header() the same zval (wrapping one zend_string, with its refcount left unchanged) is inserted into TWO independent hash tables: request.headers (keyed by the lowercased name) and request.headers_original_case (keyed by the original-case name). No Z_TRY_ADDREF is performed between the two inserts, and by design (see the ctor comment and zend_hash_init calls) only request.headers is given a destructor (cli_header_value_dtor, which calls zend_string_release_ex), while request.headers_original_case is created with a NULL destructor because it is treated as merely borrowing the same object. This ownership model is only sound as long as every value stored in headers_original_case is still owned by a live entry in headers under the matching key. That invariant breaks whenever an entry in `headers` is replaced: when a header name is sent more than once, the code either merges the values (non-Set-Cookie) or overwrites them (Set-Cookie), and the zend_hash_update on `headers` runs the destructor on the previous value, freeing that zend_string. Because `headers` is keyed by the lowercased name but `headers_original_case` is keyed by the exact bytes the client sent, a duplicate header whose two occurrences differ only in letter case produces a SINGLE merged/replaced entry in `headers` (old string freed) but TWO distinct entries in `headers_original_case`, one of which still points at the now-freed string. That entry is a dangling pointer. It is later dereferenced — and its refcount field mutated — by apache_request_headers()/getallheaders(), which calls zend_array_dup(&request.headers_original_case); zend_array_dup walks every value and bumps the refcount of each refcounted zend_string, writing into freed memory (use-after-free) and copying the stale pointer into a user-visible array, which is subsequently released, yielding a double free. The root cause is that two containers co-own one heap object while only one accounts for its lifetime and no reference count is taken.
findings.reachable_how: Fully remote and unauthenticated against the PHP built-in/development web server. The attacker simply sends an HTTP request containing the same header name twice with different capitalization (e.g. two occurrences of a header that collapse to the same lowercase key but keep distinct original-case keys). The request parser callbacks store these during normal request setup, leaving a freed/dangling pointer inside request.headers_original_case. The dangling pointer is turned into an actual use-after-free/double-free the moment the served PHP application enumerates request headers via getallheaders()/apache_request_headers() — an extremely common operation — which duplicates headers_original_case and touches the freed string.

t618.why: Finding is about header string refcounting in the CLI server, not an OOM during multipart request startup followed by cleanup of partially initialized state.

t619.why: Finding is a use-after-free within a single request from duplicate case-differing headers, not stale per-request global state surviving a fatal error and read by a later request on a reused worker via session upload progress.

findings.title: request_info.content_type_dup / current_user freed without being nulled in sapi_deactivate_module
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c request teardown (sapi_deactivate_module) vs. setup (sapi_activate)
findings.mechanism: At the end of a request sapi_deactivate_module() does `efree(SG(request_info).content_type_dup)` and `efree(SG(request_info).current_user)` but, unlike the adjacent auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest cleanup, it does NOT set these pointers back to NULL. The only thing that keeps this safe is that the next request's sapi_activate() is supposed to re-initialize them. However, that re-initialization is conditional: content_type_dup is only assigned inside the `if (SG(server_context))` block (either set by sapi_read_post_data() for a POST, or explicitly NULLed in the non-POST else branch). If a subsequent request is activated while SG(server_context) is not set at activate time (or the POST/else re-init path is otherwise skipped), the stale, already-freed pointer survives into the next request. The following sapi_deactivate_module() then sees the non-NULL dangling pointer and efree()s it again -> double free of heap memory. The same shape applies to current_user (only reset in sapi_activate, freed-not-nulled in deactivate). Because content_type_dup points at estrndup'd per-request heap, the freed chunk can be reallocated for attacker-influenced data between the two frees, turning the double free into a controllable allocator corruption.
findings.reachable_how: Reached by the normal HTTP request lifecycle on a long-lived/reused worker (FPM, CGI, embed). A POST request causes sapi_read_post_data() to estrndup content_type into content_type_dup; if the script never triggers $_POST handling (which is what nulls it via sapi_handle_post), teardown frees it without nulling. On the next request on the same worker whose activate path does not overwrite the pointer, teardown frees the same address again. No authentication is required; the attacker only controls whether a request is POST and whether it carries a Content-Type.

findings.title: SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files) overwritten without destroying the prior hash when the multipart handler runs more than once
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c (rfc1867_post_handler) + ext/standard/http.c (request_parse_body) interaction with SAPI post handling
findings.mechanism: rfc1867_post_handler() unconditionally allocates a new uploaded_files HashTable and does `SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files) = uploaded_files;` and `zend_hash_init(&PG(rfc1867_protected_variables), ...)` without first checking/destroying any existing instance. The teardown that unlinks temp files and frees the hash (destroy_uploaded_files_hash / fileupload_done) operates only on the current SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files). Because request_parse_body() calls sapi_read_post_data() again mid-request and then sapi_handle_post(), the multipart handler can execute a second time in the same request; the second run overwrites the SG pointer, orphaning the first hash (its registered temp-file zend_strings are leaked and its on-disk temp files are never unlinked). More dangerously, if a Zend memory-allocation bailout (out-of-memory / fatal) unwinds out of rfc1867_post_handler() after SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files) and PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) have been installed but before the fileupload_done cleanup runs, those process/thread-persistent globals are left referencing request-arena memory that is released at request shutdown, so the structures survive into the next request pointing at freed arena storage until re-initialized.
findings.reachable_how: A POST with multipart/form-data triggers rfc1867_post_handler during normal $_FILES/$_POST population; a script that additionally calls request_parse_body() (or any path that causes the post data to be parsed twice) reaches the double-install. The bailout variant is reachable by any unauthenticated multipart upload that drives allocation to the memory_limit while the handler is mid-parse.

findings.title: Potential size_t underflow in CLI built-in server POST reader
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c (sapi_cli_server_read_post)
findings.mechanism: The reader computes `nbytes_copied = MIN(post_read_offset + count_bytes, content_len) - post_read_offset` and then memmove()s nbytes_copied bytes from `content + post_read_offset`. The client request struct (including content, content_len and post_read_offset) is persistent and reused across keep-alive requests on the same connection. If request state is reused such that post_read_offset ever exceeds content_len (e.g., offset carried over or content replaced with a shorter body between requests on the reused client object), the subtraction underflows to a huge size_t and the memmove performs a massive out-of-bounds read/copy. Correct per-request reset of post_read_offset relative to content/content_len is the only guard.
findings.reachable_how: The CLI server is a reused-worker HTTP server reachable by any remote client; crafted sequences of requests (especially keep-alive / pipelined bodies) on the same connection exercise the persistent client content/offset fields.

findings.title: Use-after-free of request header value via headers_original_case when duplicate headers with differing letter-case are sent (CLI server)
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — HTTP request header parsing/storage (php_cli_server_client_save_header and the per-client request.headers / request.headers_original_case hashtables)
findings.mechanism: Each client keeps two persistent hashtables for request headers: `request.headers`, keyed by the lower-cased header name and owning its zend_string values (it has the destructor cli_header_value_dtor), and `request.headers_original_case`, keyed by the original-case name and deliberately registered with NO destructor because it is intended to alias the exact same value strings as `request.headers`. In php_cli_server_client_save_header(), when a header name is seen again (entry already present in `request.headers`) and it is not Set-Cookie, the code allocates a brand-new concatenated string `newval` (= old value + ", " + new value) and calls zend_hash_update(&request.headers, lc_name, newval). That update invokes the destructor on the previous value string, freeing it (its refcount was 1). It then calls zend_hash_update(&request.headers_original_case, current_header_name, newval). The critical flaw: the second hashtable is keyed by the *original-case* name. If the two occurrences of the header use different letter casing (e.g. "X-Foo:" followed by "x-FOO:"), the lower-cased key collides in `request.headers` (triggering the merge-and-free) but the original-case keys differ, so the update to `request.headers_original_case` inserts a NEW bucket for the second casing instead of overwriting the first. The first-casing bucket in `request.headers_original_case` is left pointing at the value string that was just freed by the `request.headers` destructor. Because `request.headers_original_case` has no destructor, nothing fixes or frees this entry; it simply retains a dangling pointer into freed heap memory. The aliasing invariant the code relies on (both tables point at the same live strings) is broken precisely in the case-mismatched duplicate scenario.
findings.reachable_how: A remote, unauthenticated client connected to the PHP built-in web server (php -S, used in development and sometimes exposed) fully controls request header names and values and can trivially send the same header twice with different casing, creating the dangling entry during header parsing. The freed-then-dangling value is subsequently dereferenced when any served script calls apache_request_headers()/getallheaders(), which is implemented at php_cli_server.c:419 as zend_array_dup(&client->request.headers_original_case); that dup walks every bucket and reads/copies each value zend_string, dereferencing the freed string and producing a use-after-free (information disclosure of reclaimed heap contents, and potential corruption depending on allocator reuse). No authentication or special configuration is required beyond the server serving a script that enumerates request headers.

findings.title: SAPI request teardown frees content_type_dup and current_user without nulling them (latent cross-request dangling pointer)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module()
findings.mechanism: In sapi_deactivate_module(), the authentication fields (auth_user, auth_password, auth_digest) are efree'd AND set to NULL, but the immediately following cleanup of SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user calls efree() WITHOUT resetting the pointers to NULL. This asymmetry leaves stale, freed pointers in the persistent SAPI request_info structure after a request completes. Safety against a double-free/use-after-free on the next request currently depends entirely on sapi_activate() unconditionally reassigning these fields; content_type_dup in particular is only reset inside the `if (SG(server_context))` block (either overwritten by sapi_read_post_data() for POST or set to NULL in the else branch). Any request-handling flow that reaches teardown with these fields set but does not go through that reset on the next activation (e.g. an embedding/SAPI path where server_context is not set during activation) would re-enter sapi_deactivate_module() and efree() the same dangling pointer again, yielding a double free of worker-persistent state.
findings.reachable_how: The content_type_dup field is populated directly from attacker-controlled request data (the Content-Type header) via sapi_read_post_data() on every POST request on a reused worker (FPM/embed). The missing NULL-after-free is a cross-request state-hygiene defect in the exact request setup/teardown path; it is latent for the mainstream SAPIs because activation happens to overwrite the field, but the pattern is fragile and is the kind of teardown gap that becomes an exploitable double-free as soon as an activation path skips the reset.

t619.why: The finding's use-after-free is within a single request, via aliasing hashtables. It has no stale global state surviving a fatal error across reused workers and no session upload progress path.

findings.title: Double-free / use-after-free of HTTP superglobals (PG(http_globals)) when request startup bails out before php_hash_environment on a reused worker
findings.subsystem: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown) and main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment); reachable via SAPIs that reuse a process/worker and still run request shutdown after a failed startup (e.g. the built-in cli_server, mod_php worker).
findings.mechanism: The array of per-request superglobals PG(http_globals)[] ($_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES/$_REQUEST) is torn down in php_request_shutdown step 8, which calls zval_ptr_dtor on each slot but NEVER resets the slots to IS_UNDEF afterward. After a request completes, each slot therefore still holds an IS_ARRAY zval whose backing HashTable was just freed (and, after the memory-manager reset in step 15, that memory is returned to the allocator). The ONLY place these dangling slots are made safe again is the single line 'memset(PG(http_globals), 0, sizeof(PG(http_globals)))' at the very top of php_hash_environment(). Crucially, php_hash_environment() is invoked near the END of php_request_startup(), after many operations that allocate memory and can trigger a zend_bailout on memory_limit/OOM: php_output_activate, zend_activate, sapi_activate (which may read/parse request input), the expose_php header allocation, and php_output_start_user() for output buffering. The whole body of php_request_startup runs inside a zend_try; if any of those earlier steps bails out, control jumps to zend_catch, retval becomes FAILURE, and php_hash_environment()'s memset is skipped entirely. The stale, already-freed PG(http_globals) entries from the PREVIOUS request on that same worker are left intact. When the caller then performs request shutdown, step 8 runs zval_ptr_dtor on those dangling IS_ARRAY zvals a second time — a double-free / use-after-free on attacker-influenced heap state (the freed array memory may already have been reused by allocations made during the failed startup). This is precisely the class of request-lifecycle/OOM corruption described in the circa-2004 PHP research: the reset of reused per-request global state depends on a feature that runs before application code (auto-global environment setup), and if an allocation fails before that feature runs, the stale state is destroyed twice.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated remote request drives php_request_startup on a long-lived, reused worker. SAPIs such as the built-in web server (php -S / cli_server) call php_cli_server_request_shutdown() -> php_request_shutdown() even when php_request_startup() returned FAILURE, and the same process serves the next request; mod_php Apache workers similarly persist across requests. A first (ordinary) request populates PG(http_globals); its shutdown frees them but leaves dangling IS_ARRAY zvals. A subsequent request whose startup exhausts the memory limit before php_hash_environment runs (e.g. via memory pressure created during output-buffer/header setup or input reading during sapi_activate under a constrained memory_limit) skips the memset that would have neutralized the stale pointers, and the ensuing shutdown re-destroys the freed superglobal arrays, corrupting the heap.

findings.title: Request-parse state (rfc1867 multipart handler) left partially initialized across requests when a bailout interrupts upload parsing
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c (rfc1867_post_handler) together with per-request globals PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) and SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files); runs before application code via sapi_handle_post / auto-global creation of $_POST/$_FILES.
findings.mechanism: rfc1867_post_handler installs several pieces of per-request/global state as it parses a multipart/form-data body — it zend_hash_init()s PG(rfc1867_protected_variables), ALLOC_HASHTABLE()s and assigns SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files), and builds up heap buffers (lbuf/abuf/array_index/mbuff) — all of which are only released at the single 'fileupload_done:' epilogue. The body of the parser performs a large number of emalloc/erealloc operations and multibyte conversions that can trigger a zend_bailout (memory_limit/OOM) at essentially any point. A bailout does not run the epilogue, so PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) can be left as an initialized HashTable whose bucket memory is subsequently freed wholesale by the request's memory-manager shutdown, leaving the persistent PG() struct pointing at freed storage; the parser's reliance on a single exit path for cleanup means interrupted parses do not restore the clean 'before application code' invariants that the next request's setup assumes. Because this parsing feature executes implicitly during superglobal population (before user code), the inconsistent leftover state is reached without the application ever being involved.
findings.reachable_how: Any unauthenticated POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data causes this handler to run during $_POST/$_FILES population. An attacker can shape the body (many parts, large fields, encoding conversions) to force allocation failure mid-parse, producing a bailout that bypasses the handler's cleanup epilogue; on a reused worker the half-initialized per-request parsing globals carry into the teardown/next-request path.

t618.why: The finding names an OOM/bailout during php_request_startup that skips initialization, followed by request shutdown running over invalid (stale, not-yet-reset) superglobal state. That matches both hit requirements.

t619.why: The finding describes per-request global state (http_globals) persisting after free on a reused worker and being consumed a second time via a pre-application path. That is the stale-pointer use-after-free mechanism, though it goes through shutdown rather than session upload progress.

t618.why: Describes an OOM/bailout during multipart parsing that leaves partially-initialized request state, with teardown then operating on that state.

t619.why: Mentions stale freed pointers in persistent globals on reused workers and a pre-application-code path, but never shows a later request reading the stale state (session upload progress UAF).

findings.title: Cross-request use-after-free of the HTTP superglobals (PG(http_globals)) when request startup bails out before php_hash_environment on a reused worker
findings.subsystem: Request lifecycle — main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown), main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment), main/SAPI.c (sapi_activate / sapi_read_post_data), reached via SAPIs that reuse the worker after a failed startup (sapi/apache2handler).
findings.mechanism: The six superglobal slots PG(http_globals)[] (for $_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES) are per-request global state that lives in the process-persistent PG() struct but points at arrays allocated in the per-request Zend memory-manager heap. At request teardown, php_request_shutdown() step 8 destroys them with zval_ptr_dtor(&PG(http_globals)[i]) but does NOT reset the slots to IS_UNDEF. Immediately afterwards shutdown_memory_manager() tears down the whole request heap. Consequently, after any request that populated a superglobal, the PG(http_globals)[] slots are left holding dangling IS_ARRAY zvals pointing into freed (and soon reused) heap memory. The ONLY place that re-sanitizes these stale pointers for the next request is the memset(PG(http_globals),0,...) at the top of php_hash_environment(). That memset runs late in php_request_startup() (after php_output_activate, zend_activate and, crucially, sapi_activate). sapi_activate() performs POST/body reading and parsing BEFORE php_hash_environment() is reached. If an allocation fails there — e.g. memory_limit is hit while buffering/parsing a crafted request body — a zend_bailout fires; php_request_startup() catches it and returns FAILURE, having skipped the memset. The matching php_request_shutdown() still unconditionally runs step 8 and calls zval_ptr_dtor() on the still-dangling PG(http_globals)[] slots from the previous request, operating on freed (possibly already re-allocated) memory: a refcount decrement / array destruction on a stale pointer, i.e. a use-after-free / double-free leading to heap corruption. Root cause: teardown frees the slots without nulling them, and the re-initialization that compensates for that is gated behind a startup step (php_hash_environment) that is skippable on OOM.
findings.reachable_how: No authentication required. The attacker first issues one ordinary request that causes any superglobal to be populated (normal GET/POST/cookies), leaving the PG(http_globals)[] slots dangling after that request's shutdown. Then, against a worker that is reused after a failed startup (mod_php/apache2handler runs the handler in zend_first_try and still calls php_request_shutdown via the request dtor, then serves the next request on the same thread), the attacker sends a request whose body processing exhausts memory_limit during sapi_activate()'s POST/body reading — before php_hash_environment() runs. The resulting bailout skips the memset re-init, and request shutdown then re-destroys the dangling superglobal arrays, corrupting the heap on a long-lived worker.

t618.why: OOM bailout during startup body parsing leaves state uninitialized and shutdown operates on it

t619.why: Describes stale per-request globals surviving free across reused worker requests, but not the pre-application consumer (session upload progress) or the fatal-error-interrupted cleanup mechanism

findings.title: EXIF IFD/MakerNote parser: attacker-controlled offset and byte_count arithmetic driving pointer dereferences
findings.subsystem: ext/exif/exif.c (exif_process_IFD_TAG_impl, exif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE, exif_offset_info_try_get)
findings.mechanism: The EXIF reader derives byte_count from an untrusted 32-bit component count multiplied by the per-format element size, and an untrusted 32-bit offset_val taken directly from the image. These values are then used to locate a value pointer either inside an in-memory section buffer (via exif_offset_info_try_get, which must correctly reject offset+length ranges that fall outside offset_base..offset_base+valid_length) or by seeking/reading from the stream into either a 32-byte stack buffer (cbuf) or a heap buffer sized to byte_count. The entire memory-safety of this code rests on (a) the overflow/range checks at the pointer-range test, (b) the FileSize-vs-byte_count/offset_val checks (e.g. the `offset_val > FileSize - byte_count` expression, which is only safe because of the preceding `byte_count > FileSize` guard), and (c) the per-entry bounds checks in the MakerNote dispatcher (`2 + NumDirEntries*12 > value_len` and `dir_start - value_ptr > value_len - (2+NumDirEntries*12)`). Any single off-by-one or dropped guard in this chain yields an out-of-bounds read (and, in the stream-read path, a controlled-size copy) from attacker-chosen offsets. The nested MakerNote re-entry re-bases the offset_info and reinterprets endianness, widening the set of offsets an attacker can steer the parser toward. This is the densest concentration of untrusted-length pointer arithmetic I observed and the most plausible location for a serious memory-safety defect.
findings.reachable_how: A remote, unauthenticated attacker uploads or supplies an image file (e.g. a crafted JPEG/TIFF with APP1/EXIF, or a malicious thumbnail/MakerNote). Any application that calls exif_read_data()/exif_thumbnail()/getimagesize() with EXIF info on the uploaded or fetched file drives this parser over the attacker's bytes. The image bytes fully control tag formats, component counts, and offsets consumed by the IFD walker.

findings.title: HTTP response Location header copy relies on monotonic length tracking (reviewed, appears bounded)
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/http_fopen_wrapper.c (php_stream_read_http_headers Location handling)
findings.mechanism: When following redirects, the wrapper stores each Location header value into header_info->location, reallocating only when the previously stored length is <= the new value length and otherwise reusing the existing buffer. I traced the allocate/realloc/copy interplay across repeated Location headers of varying lengths and the HTTP_HEADER_MAX_LOCATION_SIZE cap; in every ordering the destination buffer remained at least new_len+1 bytes before the memcpy of new_len+1, so I did not confirm a defect here. I flag it because it is the one remote-server-controlled copy with non-trivial length bookkeeping and would be the place to re-verify if the length-tracking invariant were ever perturbed.
findings.reachable_how: Reached via SSRF-style or legitimate use of fopen/file_get_contents/stream functions against an attacker-influenced HTTP URL with follow_location enabled; the malicious server returns crafted Location headers across redirects.

t618.why: The finding covers EXIF parser bounds arithmetic. It does not touch an OOM during request startup or cleanup of partially-initialized request state.

t619.why: The finding does not address request-global state that survives a fatal error into a reused worker, or a use-after-free via session upload progress.

findings.title: IPTC parser (iptcparse) relies on NUL-termination while scanning past examined offset
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/iptc.c, PHP_FUNCTION(iptcparse)
findings.mechanism: The hand-written parser over an attacker-supplied binary string dereferences buffer[inx+1] in its initial tag-search loop while only bounding inx (buffer[inx+1] is read when inx can be str_len-1). The length/offset checks for the record bodies (inx+4, inx+6, len>str_len, inx+len>str_len) are correct and prevent the body copy from over-reading, so the only out-of-range access is a single byte immediately after the examined position. That byte is the implicit trailing NUL of the zend_string, so in the current layout the read stays inside the allocation; the pattern is nonetheless fragile because correctness depends entirely on strings always carrying a terminating byte, and any caller passing a non-NUL-terminated buffer would get a one-byte over-read. This is the closest-to-defect construct I could confirm in a remotely reachable parser.
findings.reachable_how: iptcparse() (and the IPTC path of getimagesize()) runs on byte strings taken directly from request input or from an uploaded file; an attacker who controls the IPTC/APP13 bytes of an image that the application parses reaches this code with no authentication.

findings.title: Built-in HTTP server body buffering grows without an enforced upper bound
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c, php_cli_server_client_read_request_on_body
findings.mechanism: On the first body callback the code allocates parser->content_length bytes but sets content_len to 0, then immediately reallocates to content_len+length and memmove()s each chunk in. Each subsequent chunk reallocates to the running total. The initial content_length allocation is effectively discarded, and the accumulated size is driven by the number of body bytes actually delivered rather than validated against the declared Content-Length, so a client streaming more body than advertised (or chunked bodies) drives unbounded reallocation. This is a resource/trust concern rather than a confirmed spatial overflow (realloc tracks the true size), but it is the weakest point in the request-reading path and worth hardening.
findings.reachable_how: The php -S development server parses raw HTTP from any client; the on_body callback is invoked directly from the bundled HTTP parser for every request body, so it is reachable pre-authentication.

findings.title: Residual risk: binary-format parsers (exif, gd, phar, mbstring) not fully audited
findings.subsystem: ext/exif, ext/gd, ext/phar, ext/mbstring
findings.mechanism: These extensions contain the most complex hand-written parsing of attacker-controlled binary data (EXIF IFD traversal, image decoders, phar manifest parsing, multibyte conversion) and are historically the richest source of PHP memory-safety defects (out-of-bounds reads/writes from attacker-chosen lengths/offsets). The request-parsing and common string paths I reviewed in main/, ext/standard/string.c, ext/standard/url.c, ext/uri, and the CLI-server header handling matched safe upstream logic with proper overflow-guarded allocations (zend_string_safe_alloc, bounded port_buf copies, size checks in substr_replace/str_repeat/sprintf). Given that, the most serious reachable defect is most likely to live in one of these binary parsers, which I could not finish reading within budget.
findings.reachable_how: exif_read_data()/getimagesize() on uploaded images, Phar extraction of uploaded archives, and mbstring conversion of request strings are all commonly invoked on untrusted, unauthenticated input in typical deployments.

findings.title: Attacker-length-driven memory operations in the unserialize string handlers (var_unserializer)
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/var_unserializer.re (php_var_unserialize_internal, 's:'/'S:' string cases, unserialize_str)
findings.mechanism: The serialized-string handlers read an attacker-declared length field (parse_uiv) and then use it to drive raw pointer arithmetic over the input buffer. The 's:' case computes maxlen = max - YYCURSOR, rejects only when maxlen < len, then sets str = YYCURSOR, advances YYCURSOR += len, and immediately dereferences *(YYCURSOR) and *(YYCURSOR+1) looking for the closing '"' and ';'. Because the bound check only guarantees room for the string body and not for the two trailing delimiter bytes, the final pointer can sit at the very end of the live buffer; correctness of the subsequent dereferences depends entirely on the input zend_string's single trailing NUL byte short-circuiting before the '+1' read. Any weakening of that boundary relation (declared length vs. remaining buffer) turns this into an out-of-bounds read, and the declared length is fully attacker controlled. The 'S:' variant routes the same attacker length through unserialize_str, which must itself honor maxlen while decoding \xNN escapes into a freshly allocated buffer — an off-by-one between the allocation size and the number of decoded bytes would be a heap overflow. This is the canonical memory-safety hot spot of the interpreter because every type/length token in the stream is attacker-chosen.
findings.reachable_how: unserialize() is routinely called on request-controlled data (POST bodies, cookies, API payloads) by PHP applications, and PHP's own session subsystem deserializes session payloads whose contents can originate from client-supplied data in many configurations. A single HTTP request carrying a crafted serialized string reaches these handlers with no authentication.

findings.title: Remote input decoders operate in-place on request-controlled buffers
findings.subsystem: main/php_variables.c (php_default_treat_data, add_post_var) and ext/standard/url.c (php_url_decode_ex / php_raw_url_decode_ex)
findings.mechanism: GET/POST/COOKIE processing copies the raw request strings and performs in-place percent-decoding and '&'/'='/';' tokenization using size_t length counters and pointer walks. The decoders rely on the invariant that '%' sequences only consume two extra bytes when src_len>=2, and the POST scanner (add_post_var) relies on already_scanned never exceeding end-ptr across buffered reads. These are the first code to touch unauthenticated bytes; any arithmetic error in the remaining-length tracking (e.g., the size_t underflow idiom while(src_len--) or the already_scanned carry between smart_str appends) would corrupt the in-place decode bounds. I verified the current arithmetic appears consistent, but this is the primary unauthenticated entry surface and warrants the closest scrutiny for any regression.
findings.reachable_how: Every HTTP request automatically flows through php_default_treat_data to populate $_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE before any user script runs; no authentication or application code is required.

findings.title: Multipart/form-data parser buffer and boundary handling
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c (fill_buffer, next_line, multipart_buffer_read, rfc1867_post_handler)
findings.mechanism: The multipart engine uses a fixed int-sized ring buffer (bytes_in_buffer/bufsize) and attacker-controlled boundary strings. next_line writes line[self->bufsize]=0 at the full-buffer boundary (valid only because the buffer is over-allocated by one), multipart_buffer_read performs memcpy of up to bytes-1 and writes buf[len] plus a trailing '\r' trim, and the per-part Content-Disposition name is used to size lbuf via safe_erealloc before snprintf. The use of int for bytes_in_buffer/boundary lengths and the hand-rolled boundary search (php_ap_memstr) make this a sensitive area: an incorrect boundary-length or buffer-fill computation would yield over-reads/writes directly from the POST body. The boundary length is capped (FILLUNIT - strlen("\r\n--")) and the snprintf targets are length-bounded, so the current code appears safe, but it is fully attacker-driven.
findings.reachable_how: Any unauthenticated POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data is parsed by rfc1867_post_handler before user code executes, with attacker control over the boundary, header lines, field names, and body chunk sizes.

findings.title: multipart/form-data upload: variable-name buffer sizing and signed boundary length in rfc1867_post_handler
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c (SAPI POST handler for multipart/form-data)
findings.mechanism: The file-upload handler builds the $_FILES index names ($foo[name], $foo[full_path], $foo[tmp_name][idx], etc.) into a single reused heap buffer 'lbuf'. The buffer is (re)grown with the idiom 'if (llen < strlen(param)+MAX_SIZE_OF_INDEX+1){ llen=(int)strlen(param); lbuf=safe_erealloc(lbuf,llen,1,MAX_SIZE_OF_INDEX+1); llen+=MAX_SIZE_OF_INDEX+1; }', where llen is an unsigned int and the subsequent writes are produced with snprintf(lbuf, llen, ...). Correct operation depends on (a) llen never being truncated when strlen(param) is large, and (b) the array-upload concatenations ('%s_name[%s]', '%s[full_path][%s]', '%s[type][%s]', etc.) all fitting in strlen(param)+MAX_SIZE_OF_INDEX+1. The length bookkeeping mixes int/unsigned int with size_t strlen results, and boundary_len is handled as a signed int (strlen cast to int, compared against FILLUNIT-strlen("\r\n--")). This is the region of the code most sensitive to off-by-one / truncation mistakes, and it operates directly on attacker-supplied field names and boundary strings. Any under-sizing of lbuf (or truncation of llen) would turn the snprintf index construction into a heap overflow driven purely by the POST body.
findings.reachable_how: Reached by any unauthenticated HTTP POST with Content-Type: multipart/form-data. php_default_post_reader dispatches to rfc1867_post_handler before user script code runs, so the attacker controls the boundary, the Content-Disposition 'name' (param, including '[' array syntax), and 'filename' fields with no authentication required.

findings.title: unserialize() escaped-string ('S') and plain-string ('s') decoders rely on input NUL-termination for bounds
findings.subsystem: ext/standard/var_unserializer.re (php_var_unserialize / unserialize_str)
findings.mechanism: The 's'/'S'/'O'/'C' handlers compute len=parse_uiv(...) and maxlen=max-YYCURSOR, reject only when maxlen<len, then advance YYCURSOR by len and dereference YYCURSOR[0] and YYCURSOR[1] (checking for the closing '"' and ';'). In unserialize_str the backslash-escape branch advances the cursor up to two extra bytes and reads them without an explicit per-step bound against 'end'. Memory safety here is guaranteed only by the invariant that the serialized buffer is a NUL-terminated zend_string whose terminator sits at 'max', so any read at the boundary hits the in-bounds NUL and fails the character test. This makes the parser correct but fragile: if any caller ever passes a non-NUL-terminated buffer, or if the maxlen/len comparison is weakened, these become 1-2 byte out-of-bounds reads on every element. unserialize of attacker data is the single most common remote memory-corruption surface in PHP, so this logic warrants the strongest scrutiny.
findings.reachable_how: unserialize() is routinely invoked on unauthenticated input by web applications (and by the session subsystem via the 'php'/'php_serialize' session handlers on session cookie/body data), so a remote attacker controls the entire serialized byte stream that drives these cursor/length computations.

t618.why: Right region (multipart parsing in rfc1867), but the finding describes lbuf sizing/truncation overflow, not an OOM during request startup that leaves cleanup running over partially-initialized state.

findings.title: Use-after-free of HTTP header value strings in the built-in web server (shared single-owner string across two hashtables)
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — php_cli_server_client_save_header() and the request header hashtables (request.headers / request.headers_original_case), managed by php_cli_server_request_ctor()/_dtor() per request
findings.mechanism: Each parsed header value is wrapped in a zval (ZVAL_STR of client->current_header_value, or of a freshly allocated merged string 'newval') and then inserted into TWO hashtables via back-to-back zend_hash_update() calls: into request.headers (keyed by the lower-cased name) and into request.headers_original_case (keyed by the original-case name). No reference-count increment is performed between the two insertions, so a single zend_string with refcount 1 ends up owned by two different containers. The two tables have asymmetric destructors: request.headers is created with the value destructor cli_header_value_dtor, while request.headers_original_case is created with a NULL destructor, so the design intends 'headers' to be the sole owner and 'headers_original_case' to hold only a borrowed pointer. That invariant breaks when a client sends the same header name more than once (non 'Set-Cookie'): on the repeat, the code allocates a merged 'newval' and does zend_hash_update() on request.headers for the lower-cased key, which REPLACES the previous value and runs cli_header_value_dtor on it — freeing the old string. But request.headers_original_case still holds that old string pointer (it was inserted under the original-case key, and if the two occurrences differ in letter case the original-case key is different, so the stale entry is not overwritten). request.headers_original_case is now left with a dangling pointer to freed memory. That freed value is subsequently read/duplicated (e.g. when the headers array is materialized for the script via apache_request_headers()/getallheaders(), which does zend_array_dup() over headers_original_case and increfs/copies each value) and again during teardown ordering, yielding a use-after-free (read of freed zend_string header, refcount manipulation on freed memory, and potential freeing inconsistencies). The underlying defect is the missing refcount ownership for the second container combined with the replace-on-duplicate free path.
findings.reachable_how: The PHP built-in/development web server (php -S) accepts unauthenticated HTTP connections directly. The request bytes are fed to the embedded HTTP parser, whose on_header_field/on_header_value callbacks populate current_header_name/current_header_value and call php_cli_server_client_save_header(). An attacker simply sends a request containing the same header name twice using different letter casing (and any later access that turns headers into a PHP array, or normal request teardown) to drive the duplicate-merge code path, free the value still referenced by headers_original_case, and trigger the use-after-free. No authentication or script cooperation beyond the normal request handling is required.

findings.title: Unbounded Content-Length accumulation without overflow check feeding request-body allocation
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_http_parser.c (h_content_length state) together with sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c on_body handler
findings.mechanism: The header parser accumulates Content-Length with 'parser->content_length = parser->content_length*10 + (ch-'0')' with no overflow guard. A hostile Content-Length can overflow the signed 64-bit field to a negative/garbage value. The first invocation of the on_body callback allocates the body buffer with pemalloc(parser->content_length, ...), i.e. it uses this attacker-influenced, potentially negative value (interpreted as an enormous size_t) as the allocation size, so allocation size is driven directly by untrusted header arithmetic rather than by the actually-received body length. While the subsequent perealloc to content_len+length re-sizes to the real amount, using a corrupted content_length as the initial allocation size is an unsafe size computation on attacker-controlled data.
findings.reachable_how: Reachable over an unauthenticated HTTP connection to the built-in web server by sending a POST (or any body-bearing request) with a crafted/oversized Content-Length header; the parser processes it before any application code runs.

t618.why: Finding is about a header refcount/duplicate-merge UAF in the CLI server, not an OOM during request startup followed by cleanup of partially-initialized state.

t619.why: No stale per-request global state that survives a fatal error into a later request on a reused worker, and no session upload progress path; the UAF stays within a single request's header tables.
