t619.why: No stale global state, no use-after-free across requests on a reused worker, and no session upload progress path.

findings.title: Use-after-free of request header value via case-differing duplicate headers in the built-in web server
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — HTTP request header parsing/teardown (php_cli_server_client_save_header, apache_request_headers/getallheaders, php_cli_server_request_dtor)
findings.mechanism:
Each incoming HTTP request keeps two parallel hash tables for headers: request.headers (keyed by the lower-cased field name, initialized WITH a value destructor cli_header_value_dtor that calls zend_string_release_ex) and request.headers_original_case (keyed by the original-case field name, initialized with a NULL destructor). The design invariant, stated in a code comment, is that every value pointer stored in headers_original_case is the identical zend_string also stored in headers, so it only needs to be freed once (through the headers table). The value string is inserted into BOTH tables with ZVAL_STR and no reference-count increment, so its refcount stays 1 while two tables point at it.

When the client sends two header lines whose names are equal after lower-casing but differ in letter case (e.g. 'Foo:' then 'foo:'), save_header processes the second line: it finds the existing entry in request.headers under the shared lower-cased key and, for mergeable headers, builds a new combined string, then calls zend_hash_update on request.headers with the lower-cased key. That update replaces the old value and invokes cli_header_value_dtor, freeing the original string (refcount 1 -> freed). The subsequent zend_hash_update into headers_original_case uses the CURRENT header's original-case spelling as the key, which is a different key than the first header's spelling. Consequently the first header's original-case entry is never updated and is left pointing at the just-freed string. The two-table invariant is broken and headers_original_case now holds a dangling pointer.

The dangling pointer is dereferenced when userland PHP calls apache_request_headers()/getallheaders(), which does zend_array_dup(&client->request.headers_original_case). Duplicating the array walks every stored value and ref-counts/copies it, reading (and writing the refcount field of) the freed zend_string and propagating the freed pointer into a value handed back to the script — a classic use-after-free (read of freed memory, refcount corruption, and a live reference to freed storage). The mergeable-header path also leaks the incoming current_header_value when it builds a combined string, a secondary lifetime defect, but the memory-safety issue is the orphaned freed value in the original-case table.
findings.reachable_how: The PHP built-in web server (php -S) parses raw HTTP requests from any client that can reach the listening socket; no authentication is involved. An unauthenticated remote request need only include two header lines with the same name but different capitalization. The request header tables are populated during request set-up and are torn down per connection; the freed value becomes reachable the moment the served script invokes getallheaders()/apache_request_headers() (very common in apps that inspect request headers), triggering zend_array_dup over the corrupted headers_original_case table.

t618.why: Finding is about duplicate-header handling in the CLI server, not OOM during multipart request startup or cleanup over partially-initialized state.

t619.why: Finding is a within-request UAF on header values; it does not involve stale global state surviving across requests on a reused worker or session upload progress.

findings.title: Fixed stack buffers for REMOTE_ADDR/REMOTE_PORT in built-in server var registration
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — sapi_cli_server_register_variables()
findings.mechanism: When the built-in web server builds the $_SERVER superglobal for a request, it splits the stored client address string (client->addr_str) on the last ':' and copies the address part and port part into two fixed on-stack buffers: char addr[64] and char port[8]. The address portion is copied with strncpy(addr, addr_start, addr_len) where addr_len = addr_end - addr_start is computed directly from the stored string, and is then NUL-terminated with addr[addr_len] = '\0'. There is no check that addr_len is strictly less than sizeof(addr). If addr_len equals 64 the terminating write addr[64] is one byte past the buffer, and if it exceeds 64 the strncpy itself overruns the stack frame. The ZEND_ASSERT(addr_len == strlen(addr)) that follows is compiled out in release builds and provides no protection. The same pattern (fixed port[8] with strncpy of up to 8 bytes) relies on the manual port[7]='\0' to stay safe. This is a classic missing-length-validation stack write where the destination size is a hard-coded constant but the source length is taken from an externally-populated string rather than bounded against the buffer.
findings.reachable_how: The function runs for every request served by the PHP built-in web server (php -S) while materializing $_SERVER, i.e. during request state setup before the script runs. It executes on a connection established by any remote, unauthenticated client. The length that is copied is derived from the textual peer-address string associated with the accepted connection; any path that causes that string to be longer than the fixed buffers (e.g. long IPv6 textual forms including zone/scope identifiers, or any configuration/transport that yields an oversized address string) turns the unchecked copy into an out-of-bounds stack write reachable purely by connecting and issuing a request.

findings.title: Request-line/URI and query-string length bounds enforced only by debug-only assertions
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — on_url()/on_query_string() request parser callbacks
findings.mechanism: As the HTTP request line is parsed incrementally, the on_url and on_query_string callbacks append fragments to persistent buffers. The invariant that the accumulated length stays within PHP_HTTP_MAX_HEADER_SIZE is expressed with ZEND_ASSERT(...) statements (e.g. that length <= PHP_HTTP_MAX_HEADER_SIZE and that the remaining capacity is sufficient). These assertions are no-ops in a normal (NDEBUG) build. While the concatenation helpers themselves reallocate dynamically, the code's correctness reasoning for bounding attacker-controlled growth of these persistent request buffers depends on the parser's nread/PHP_HTTP_MAX_HEADER_SIZE guard applying to the request-line states; if that guard does not cover the URL/query-string accumulation states the only remaining limit is the debug assertion, allowing unbounded attacker-driven growth of request state during setup. This is a robustness/defense-in-depth weakness in the request-lifecycle setup path rather than a confirmed single overflow.
findings.reachable_how: Reached by any remote client sending an HTTP request with a long request target to the built-in server; the callbacks fire during request parsing (state setup) before dispatch.

t618.why: The finding is a stack buffer overflow in CLI server address parsing. It involves no OOM during request startup and no cleanup over partially-initialized state.

t619.why: The finding does not involve stale per-request global state, a use-after-free across reused workers, or session upload progress.

t618.why: The finding is about unbounded URL/query buffer growth guarded only by debug asserts in the CLI server parser. It does not involve an OOM during multipart parsing or cleanup over partially-initialized request state.

t619.why: There is no stale per-request global state, no use-after-free across reused workers, and no session upload progress path.

findings.title: Dangling request_info pointers after per-request SAPI teardown (content_type_dup / current_user not NULLed)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module() / sapi_activate() / sapi_handle_post()
findings.mechanism: During request teardown, sapi_deactivate_module() efree()s several SG(request_info) string fields but is inconsistent about clearing them. auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest are freed AND set to NULL, but content_type_dup (freed at line ~526-528) and current_user (freed at line ~529-531) are freed WITHOUT being reset to NULL. The code's safety therefore depends entirely on every subsequent code path re-initializing these pointers before the next free or use. content_type_dup is additionally freed in two other places (sapi_handle_post() sets it NULL after freeing; sapi_read_post_data() assigns a fresh buffer). If any request path reaches a second free or a read of these fields while they still hold a stale (already-freed) address — e.g. an early-error or non-standard request-method flow where sapi_activate() does not go through sapi_read_post_data() to overwrite content_type_dup, or where sapi_initialize_empty_request()/partial re-entry leaves the stale value — the freed pointer is dereferenced or passed to efree() again, producing a use-after-free / double-free of heap memory whose contents are attacker-influenced (the Content-Type string / authenticated user name derived from request headers).
findings.reachable_how: All of these fields are populated directly from untrusted request metadata: content_type_dup comes from the client Content-Type header (sapi_read_post_data), and current_user/auth_* come from request/authorization headers. They are set up in sapi_activate() at the start of every request and torn down in sapi_deactivate_module() at the end, so the lifecycle is driven entirely by an unauthenticated remote request. The inconsistency (some fields NULLed, these not) is the classic precondition for a dangling-pointer defect across the setup/teardown boundary.

findings.title: POST/multipart request-body parsing surface (defense-in-depth review)
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c and main/php_variables.c (php_std_post_handler / add_post_var / rfc1867_post_handler)
findings.mechanism: These routines run before any user script, parsing attacker-controlled request bodies into heap buffers with repeated erealloc/estrndup/memmove and manual length bookkeeping (e.g. the add_post_var already_scanned/memmove logic, the rfc1867 lbuf sizing against MAX_SIZE_OF_INDEX, and multipart_buffer_read's boundary scan). In this checkout the bounds arithmetic matches the known-good upstream implementation, but this is the highest-value attack surface for memory-safety regressions because every byte and length is attacker-chosen and the code mixes signed int and size_t lengths; any off-by-one in the lbuf realloc condition or the boundary/partial-match accounting would become a remotely reachable heap overflow.
findings.reachable_how: Reached by any unauthenticated POST request with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data; the handlers are invoked automatically from sapi_activate()/php_hash_environment() during request startup, prior to authentication or application logic.

t618.why: Targets request startup/teardown in SAPI and partial-state cleanup but never names the OOM/allocation failure trigger or multipart parsing.

t619.why: Describes stale freed request_info pointers surviving teardown, but not a fatal error interrupting cleanup, nor a later request on a reused worker reading them through session upload progress.

t618.why: Points at multipart parsing during request startup, but describes bounds/off-by-one overflow risk. It does not cover the OOM abort or cleanup over partially-initialized state.

t619.why: Does not mention stale global state surviving a free, use-after-free across requests, or session upload progress on a reused worker.

findings.title: content_type_dup freed-but-not-nulled on request teardown; not re-cleared by the headers-only activation path (stale/double-free across reused requests)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — SAPI request setup/teardown (sapi_activate / sapi_activate_headers_only / sapi_read_post_data / sapi_handle_post / sapi_deactivate_module)
findings.mechanism: For a POST request, sapi_read_post_data() estrdup()s the content type into SG(request_info).content_type_dup and leaves it live for the duration of the request. The pointer is consumed in one of two ways: sapi_handle_post() efree()s it and sets it to NULL (only if $_POST is actually parsed), and sapi_deactivate_module() efree()s it at request teardown but does NOT reset it to NULL. The full sapi_activate() re-arms this field each request (it is overwritten by sapi_read_post_data() for POSTs, or explicitly set to NULL in the non-POST branch), which normally masks the missing reset. However, the alternate activation entry point sapi_activate_headers_only() carefully re-clears many SG(request_info) fields (post_entry, request_body, current_user, etc.) but never touches content_type_dup. Consequently, on a long-lived/reused worker, a request that went through the full activate path and left a dangling (already-efree()d, not-NULLed) content_type_dup pointer can be followed by a request that activates via the headers-only path; that path leaves the stale pointer in place, and the subsequent sapi_deactivate_module() sees content_type_dup != NULL and efree()s it again — a double free of a heap pointer whose value is leftover request state. The same not-nulled-after-free pattern exists for current_user in sapi_deactivate_module(), but current_user is re-cleared in both activation paths, so content_type_dup is the asymmetric case. The root cause is freeing request-scoped heap pointers without nulling them, combined with two activation paths that do not reset the identical set of fields.
findings.reachable_how: SG(request_info).content_type is attacker-controlled: it is the Content-Type request header. Sending a POST with a Content-Type drives sapi_read_post_data() to allocate content_type_dup. Whether it is cleared depends on whether the script reads $_POST, which the attacker influences via the target endpoint. On persistent-worker SAPIs (FastCGI/FPM, or any SAPI that uses the headers-only activation path for some requests), successive unauthenticated HTTP requests run in the same process with the SG(request_info) structure reused, so leftover state from one request is observable by the next, turning the missing NULL reset into a cross-request double-free primitive.

findings.title: rfc1867 per-request hashtable PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) is initialized mid-handler and only torn down at the very end, so a mid-request allocation bailout leaves engine-global state pointing at freed memory
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c — multipart/form-data POST handler (rfc1867_post_handler) and main/php_globals.h
findings.mechanism: rfc1867_post_handler() calls zend_hash_init(&PG(rfc1867_protected_variables), ...) partway through processing (after boundary validation) and only destroys it at the fileupload_done cleanup tail via zend_hash_destroy(&PG(rfc1867_protected_variables)). The large body between these points performs many heap allocations (emalloc/estrdup/erealloc for header parsing, filename/param handling, lbuf growth, temp-file bookkeeping). Any of those allocations failing triggers a Zend out-of-memory bailout (longjmp) that unwinds straight past the fileupload_done label, so the zend_hash_destroy() is skipped. PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) is an engine global embedded by value in php_globals; after the bailout, request shutdown tears down the memory manager, freeing the hashtable's backing arData, but the global struct is left in an 'initialized' state with a dangling internal pointer, and nothing in request shutdown destroys this particular hashtable. On a reused worker the next multipart POST re-enters rfc1867_post_handler and re-inits the same global, which mostly overwrites the stale pointers, but the window where the global references freed arData (and the absence of any shutdown-time reset) is fragile request-persistent state driven entirely by attacker body content. The underlying defect is that request-scoped cleanup for this global lives only on the normal-return path of a single handler rather than in request teardown, so an allocation failure mid-parse leaves global state inconsistent between requests.
findings.reachable_how: Any unauthenticated HTTP POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data reaches rfc1867_post_handler during request activation (sapi_read_post_data path). An attacker controls the body size and structure (number of parts, header sizes, filename/field-name lengths), and can drive memory pressure against memory_limit so that an allocation partway through parsing fails and bails out, exercising the skipped-cleanup path on a persistent worker.

t618.why: No allocation failure/OOM during request startup and no cleanup of partially-initialized state.

t619.why: Covers request-scoped SG state freed without nulling and persisting across reused workers. However, it names content_type_dup and a headers-only path rather than fatal-error-interrupted cleanup read by a pre-app feature like session upload progress.

t618.why: Names an allocation failure/OOM bailout during multipart parsing at request startup that leaves state partially initialized, with cleanup and shutdown inconsistent.

t619.why: Points to request-global state left dangling across a reused worker after a bailout, but says re-init overwrites it. It never shows a later read of the stale pointer via session upload progress or another pre-application path.

findings.title: Use-after-free of request header value via desynchronized dual header maps (CLI/built-in server)
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c — HTTP request parser header storage (php_cli_server_client_save_header and request lifetime structures)
findings.mechanism: Each client request keeps two hash tables for incoming headers: request.headers, keyed by the lower-cased header name and initialized WITH a value destructor (cli_header_value_dtor, which calls zend_string_release on each stored value), and request.headers_original_case, keyed by the exact client-supplied casing and initialized with NO destructor. The same header value zend_string is stored into both tables, but it is stored with ZVAL_STR (a borrow, no refcount increment), so the string has refcount 1 and is considered 'owned' only by request.headers while request.headers_original_case merely holds a borrowed pointer. The design is only safe as long as both tables hold identical value pointers under corresponding keys. When the same header name is sent more than once but with different letter casing (e.g. 'Foo:' then 'fOo:'), save_header finds the existing entry in request.headers via the lower-cased key and builds a new concatenated string; zend_hash_update on request.headers then runs the destructor on the previous value string, freeing it. The matching update into request.headers_original_case uses the ORIGINAL-case key, which differs between the two occurrences, so instead of overwriting the earlier slot it inserts a second entry. The earlier original-case slot is left pointing at the string that request.headers just freed. Because request.headers_original_case has no destructor and is never reconciled, that slot becomes a dangling pointer to freed heap memory. Any later traversal of the original-case table (e.g. exposing original-cased request headers to the script, or during request teardown/logging) dereferences the freed zend_string, i.e. a use-after-free; the concatenation path can also be driven repeatedly to groom the freed allocation.
findings.reachable_how: Fully remote and unauthenticated: the server accepts a TCP connection and feeds the raw bytes to the HTTP parser, whose on_header_field/on_header_value callbacks populate these tables with no authentication. An attacker simply sends a request containing the same header name twice using different capitalization. The worker process is long-lived and reused for many connections, so the freed-memory pointer and subsequent dereference occur while handling attacker-controlled input.

findings.title: Request-info pointers freed without being cleared on teardown
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module
findings.mechanism: During request teardown sapi_deactivate_module calls efree() on SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user without setting the pointers back to NULL afterward (unlike the auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest cases just above, which do null out the fields). This leaves dangling pointers in the per-process SAPI globals after a request completes. The values happen to be re-initialized by sapi_activate at the start of the next request on a reused worker, so in the normal startup/shutdown ordering the stale pointers are overwritten before use; however, the pattern is fragile: any SAPI or error path that reaches a second teardown, or that inspects request_info between teardown and the next activate, would operate on freed memory (double-free / use-after-free). This is a latent lifetime-management defect in the request setup/teardown path and is the kind of residual-state hazard that becomes exploitable when combined with early-exit or reuse paths.
findings.reachable_how: The request lifecycle (activate on request start, deactivate on request end) runs for every remote request on persistent worker SAPIs. The freed-but-not-nulled fields derive from attacker-influenced request metadata (Content-Type header drives content_type_dup); reachability of an actual dereference depends on the SAPI's teardown/reuse ordering, which is why it is reported as a secondary, lower-confidence concern alongside the primary finding.

t618.why: Finding describes a CLI server header-map UAF, not an OOM during request startup followed by cleanup over partially-initialized state.

t619.why: The dangling pointer lives inside a single request's header tables. There is no request-owned global state surviving a fatal error into a later request via session upload progress.

t618.why: Says nothing about an allocation failure or OOM during request startup that leaves state partially initialized before cleanup.

t619.why: Right area (per-request globals freed but not reset, stale on a reused worker), but admits next activate overwrites them and never names the fatal-error interruption or the pre-application path (session upload progress) that triggers the use-after-free.

findings.title: Request-info pointers freed but not NULLed at request teardown (stale pointer reuse across pooled workers)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module() / sapi_deactivate_destroy() vs. sapi_activate()
findings.mechanism: At the end of a request sapi_deactivate_module() does efree(SG(request_info).content_type_dup) and efree(SG(request_info).current_user) but, unlike the auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest cases right above them, it does NOT reset those two fields to NULL. sapi_deactivate_destroy() likewise does not clear them. The interpreter therefore relies entirely on the *next* request's sapi_activate() to overwrite the dangling pointer before it is used. That overwrite is conditional: content_type_dup is only re-initialised on the POST path (via sapi_read_post_data, which assigns the fresh estrndup'd buffer) or in the explicit else branch for non-POST; current_user is set to NULL unconditionally in sapi_activate but is consumed by code that runs during the window. Whenever the sequence of per-request callbacks does not deterministically re-initialise the field before it is dereferenced/freed again (e.g. a content-type whose post-entry/default-reader path leaves content_type_dup set and unfreed by sapi_handle_post, so it survives into deactivate and is efree'd a second time on an already-freed pointer, or is read by a later consumer), the stale pointer into the previous request's freed emalloc arena is used. On a reused worker the previous request's heap has already been torn down by the request memory manager, so the pointer references reclaimed memory, giving a use-after-free / double-free of attacker-influenced request-scoped data.
findings.reachable_how: Both fields are populated directly from untrusted request data on every request: content_type_dup derives from the client Content-Type header (sapi_read_post_data), and current_user/auth_* derive from the Authorization header (php_handle_auth_data). A remote, unauthenticated client fully controls whether a POST body/content-type is present and which content-type handler path runs, i.e. it controls which activate branch executes next and therefore whether the stale pointer is overwritten before reuse. Under FPM/FastCGI/LiteSpeed the same OS process handles many consecutive requests, so the teardown-without-NULL on request N and the conditional re-init on request N+1 occur in the same address space, which is exactly the cross-request reuse condition needed.

findings.title: rfc1867 multipart POST handler is not bail-out-safe; a mid-parse allocation failure skips cleanup of request globals
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c — rfc1867_post_handler()
findings.mechanism: rfc1867_post_handler() installs process/request-visible state early: it zend_hash_init()s PG(rfc1867_protected_variables), ALLOC_HASHTABLE()s uploaded_files and publishes it via SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files), and array_init()s $_FILES. All subsequent cleanup (zend_hash_destroy of the protected-variables table, freeing the multipart_buffer, freeing lbuf/abuf/array_index) happens only if control reaches the fileupload_done label at the bottom. The body of the function performs many emalloc/erealloc/estrdup/spprintf allocations and multibyte conversions that, on allocation failure, do not return an error but longjmp via zend_bailout — and the function is not wrapped in zend_try. A bail-out therefore unwinds straight past fileupload_done, leaving PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) initialised-but-not-destroyed and SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files)/the multipart buffer in a partially-constructed state. On the next request on the same worker the handler re-runs zend_hash_init() over the already-initialised PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) field, overwriting the old table bucket pointers without destroying them, and operates on globals left dangling from the aborted request, leading to leaked/mismatched allocations and dangling global state that can be dereferenced during later processing or shutdown.
findings.reachable_how: Any unauthenticated POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data drives this handler. The attacker controls the number/size of parts, field-name and filename lengths, and encoding, i.e. the total request-memory pressure, so an attacker can drive an allocation to the memory_limit/OOM boundary at a chosen point mid-parse to trigger the zend_bailout that skips the handler's manual cleanup, then issue a follow-up request on the pooled worker.

findings.title: FastCGI name/value and hash routines dereference unchecked malloc() results
findings.subsystem: main/fastcgi.c — fcgi_hash_init/fcgi_hash_set/fcgi_hash_strndup
findings.mechanism: The FastCGI request/env machinery uses raw malloc() for its persistent bucket blocks and data segments (fcgi_hash_init, the bucket-block growth in fcgi_hash_set, and the segment growth in fcgi_hash_strndup) and immediately writes through the returned pointer (p->idx, p->pos, memcpy into ret) without checking for NULL. These structures are grown in response to the attacker-supplied FCGI_PARAMS stream, where the number and sizes of name/value pairs are controlled by the request. Under memory pressure a failed malloc yields a NULL dereference; more importantly the segment/bucket objects persist in the fcgi_request across keep-alive requests, so a partial failure while populating them leaves the reused per-process request object in an inconsistent state for subsequent requests.
findings.reachable_how: Reached directly from the network by a FastCGI front-end forwarding a client request: fcgi_read_request()/fcgi_get_params() parse the attacker-influenced PARAMS and call fcgi_hash_set()/fcgi_hash_strndup() with lengths and counts taken from the request, with the fcgi_request object reused for the next request on the same worker.

t618.why: The finding does not involve an allocation failure or OOM during request startup, nor cleanup over partially-initialized state.

t619.why: It is in the right area: request-scoped global pointers reused across requests on a pooled worker, leading to use-after-free. But it blames missing NULLing in normal teardown rather than a fatal error interrupting cleanup, and it does not name a pre-application-code consumer such as session upload progress.

t618.why: The finding identifies an OOM bailout during multipart parsing that leaves request globals partially initialized and uncleaned, and says later shutdown or processing operates on that invalid state.

t619.why: It mentions dangling globals that persist into the next request on a reused worker, but it does not identify a use-after-free of freed state read through a pre-application path such as session upload progress.

t618.why: Mentions an allocation failure leaving request structures inconsistent, but the location is the FastCGI params hash. It does not cover request startup/shutdown cleanup over partially-initialized state or multipart parsing.

t619.why: Mentions per-process request state reused across keep-alive requests on a worker, but describes no use-after-free of stale global state after a fatal error and no session upload progress path.

findings.title: rfc1867 protected-variables HashTable is torn down only on the handler's normal path, leaving a dangling cross-request structure after a mid-request bailout
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c (multipart/form-data POST handler) interacting with per-process PG() globals
findings.mechanism: At the top of rfc1867_post_handler the code does zend_hash_init(&PG(rfc1867_protected_variables), ...) and also allocates SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files). PG(rfc1867_protected_variables) is a HashTable *embedded* in the per-process php_globals structure, but its backing storage (arData) is allocated from the per-request (emalloc) arena. The only place this hash is destroyed is at the fileupload_done label (zend_hash_destroy near the end of the function). It is NOT torn down in php_request_shutdown. If any allocation inside the handler fails and triggers a zend_bailout (OOM / memory_limit), or the request hits the execution-time/max_input_time timeout while the handler is running, control longjmps past fileupload_done and the zend_hash_destroy is skipped. The embedded HashTable struct therefore keeps pointers (arData etc.) into request-arena memory that is freed when the request's memory manager is shut down. Because the struct itself lives in the per-process globals of a reused worker (FPM/CGI/Apache), those stale pointers survive into the next request. On a subsequent multipart POST the handler re-runs zend_hash_init over the struct, which masks the issue in the common case, but the window between a bailed request and the next re-init is a classic use-after-free / dangling-global condition, and SG(rfc1867_uploaded_files)'s lifetime has the same fragility (it is only reliably reclaimed by sapi_deactivate_destroy, which itself runs inside zend_try during shutdown).
findings.reachable_how: Fully remote and unauthenticated: any POST with Content-Type: multipart/form-data drives sapi_read_post_data -> rfc1867_post_handler. An attacker controls body size and part count, so forcing the per-request allocator to the memory_limit (or exceeding max_input_time) during the handler is straightforward, producing the bailout that skips the normal cleanup.

findings.title: SAPI request_info string fields are freed on deactivate without being nulled, relying on activate to reset them
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c (sapi_deactivate_module / sapi_activate / sapi_handle_post)
findings.mechanism: sapi_deactivate_module() calls efree() on SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user but does not set them to NULL afterward (unlike auth_user/auth_password/auth_digest a few lines above, which are freed AND nulled). The code depends on sapi_activate() to re-establish a valid value next request. However content_type_dup is only reset inside the `if (SG(server_context))` block (either assigned by sapi_read_post_data() for a POST or explicitly set to NULL in the else branch). If a subsequent request is activated while server_context is not set, content_type_dup retains the already-freed pointer from the previous request, and the next sapi_deactivate_module() efree()s it again — a double free; any code reading it in between dereferences freed memory. The missing NULL also interacts badly with partial request startup: if php_request_startup() bails during sapi_activate() (e.g. OOM while buffering POST data in sapi_read_standard_form_data) after content_type_dup was set, the subsequent shutdown frees it but leaves the stale pointer in the long-lived SG() of a reused worker.
findings.reachable_how: Reachable through normal request processing on a persistent worker: the content_type_dup / POST reading path is driven entirely by attacker-supplied Content-Type and request body with no authentication. The dangling/double-free window is opened by forcing an allocation failure (memory_limit) during POST buffering, which an unauthenticated client can induce via a large or crafted body.

findings.title: Partial module activation on a startup bailout can skip RSHUTDOWN while leaving per-request module state allocated in a reused worker
findings.subsystem: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown)
findings.mechanism: php_request_startup() performs zend_activate_modules() and only afterwards sets PG(modules_activated)=1, all inside a single zend_try. If an allocation fails (bailout) part-way through activating modules — i.e. some extensions have already run their RINIT and allocated per-request globals, but the flag was never set — php_request_shutdown() guards the RSHUTDOWN / shutdown-function / post-deactivate steps with `if (PG(modules_activated))` and therefore skips them. Extensions that allocated and stored pointers in their per-process module globals during the RINIT that did run are never given their RSHUTDOWN to free/null those pointers. On the next request handled by the same worker, those globals still reference the previous request's (now reclaimed) arena memory, i.e. request-scoped state leaks forward into the next request as dangling state.

findings.title: Super-global state (PG(http_globals)) is reset only by the next request's startup, enabling a cross-request double-free when startup aborts (e.g. OOM) before that reset
findings.subsystem: Request lifecycle: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown) and main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment)
findings.mechanism: The six super-globals ($_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES) live in the persistent per-process/per-thread array PG(http_globals)[6]. At request shutdown, step 8 of php_request_shutdown() iterates the array calling zval_ptr_dtor(&PG(http_globals)[i]) but never writes IS_UNDEF back into those slots. Because each super-global also carries an extra reference held by EG(symbol_table), the zval_ptr_dtor in step 8 usually only decrements the refcount; the backing HashTable is actually freed slightly later when zend_deactivate() tears down the symbol table (step 9) and, ultimately, when the request memory manager is shut down (step 15). After shutdown, PG(http_globals)[i] therefore still contains a zval whose type tag is IS_ARRAY but whose pointer references freed request memory. The ONLY thing that sanitizes these stale slots for the next request is the unconditional memset(PG(http_globals), 0, sizeof(PG(http_globals))) performed at the very top of php_hash_environment(), which runs late in php_request_startup() (after sapi_activate(), output-handler startup, zend_activate(), etc.). If the next request's startup bails out (zend_bailout from an out-of-memory / memory_limit condition, or any fatal error) BEFORE control reaches php_hash_environment(), the memset is skipped. The subsequent php_request_shutdown() then re-runs step 8 over PG(http_globals) and calls zval_ptr_dtor on the already-freed zvals, producing a double-free / use-after-free of attacker-influenced heap data. This is exactly the 'per-request global state reused across requests via a feature that runs before application code' pattern (the super-global/GPC parsing machinery), and it is specifically sensitive to out-of-memory handling during request startup.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated client drives a worker that is reused across requests and that still runs request shutdown after a failed request startup (the apache2handler path is the clearest: php_apache_request_ctor() calls php_request_startup(); on FAILURE it zend_bailout()s, which is caught by the surrounding zend_first_try, and php_request_shutdown() is then invoked while the same process/thread goes on to serve further requests). A first normal request populates and later frees the super-globals, leaving stale IS_ARRAY zvals in PG(http_globals). A following request is crafted to exhaust memory during the early part of startup, before php_hash_environment() runs \u2014 for example by submitting a POST body that is read/buffered inside sapi_activate() (sapi_read_post_data \u2192 the standard form-data reader buffers the body into a temp stream and allocates per block) so that the memory_limit is hit there and a bailout occurs before the memset. The ensuing shutdown destroys the already-freed super-global arrays a second time.m

This is the modern manifestation of the circa-2004 'request-parsing state / memory_limit' problem where a bailout during variable registration leaves the request's global parse state inconsistent.
findings.reachable_how: Remote, unauthenticated: the attacker simply sends a request whose query string / cookies / POST body contain enough encoded variables to drive allocation to the memory_limit while the super-globals are being built before any PHP user code runs. findings.title: Dangling superglobal arrays (PG(http_globals)) double-freed when OOM bails out request startup before php_hash_environment on a reused worker
findings.subsystem: Request lifecycle: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown), main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment), and reused-worker SAPIs (sapi/apache2handler/sapi_apache2.c).
findings.mechanism: PG(http_globals)[] is the array of request-parsing superglobals ($_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES/$_REQUEST). Its lifecycle is asymmetric. On teardown, php_request_shutdown step 8 (main.c:2011-2018) calls zval_ptr_dtor on each PG(http_globals)[i] but never resets the slots to IS_UNDEF; the backing arrays are then actually freed when zend_deactivate() (step 9) destroys EG(symbol_table), which holds the other reference. After a completed request the slots therefore keep type IS_ARRAY while their payload pointers are dangling. The only code that re-initializes these slots to a clean state is the single memset(PG(http_globals),0,...) at main/php_variables.c:787 inside php_hash_environment(). Crucially, php_hash_environment() is called LATE in php_request_startup() (main.c:1942) — after zend_activate(), sapi_activate(), output-buffer startup, and the expose_php header, all of which perform emalloc()s wrapped only by the function's own zend_try. If any of those allocations fails (memory_limit reached), the resulting zend_bailout is caught internally and php_request_startup() returns FAILURE, but PG(http_globals)[] was never memset and still holds the previous request's dangling IS_ARRAY zvals. When the SAPI then runs php_request_shutdown() anyway, step 8 again calls zval_ptr_dtor on those dangling IS_ARRAY slots, decrementing a refcount on / freeing already-freed memory — a use-after-free / double-free whose freed object (a HashTable the attacker populated via request variables) and refcount manipulation are attacker-influenced. Because zend_activate() rebuilds a fresh empty EG(symbol_table) at the start of the failed request, PG(http_globals) is the sole remaining (dangling) reference, so the stale dtor operates directly on reclaimed heap.
findings.reachable_how: A remote, unauthenticated client drives a persistent worker (e.g., mod_php/apache2handler, which keeps the child alive and, on a failed php_request_startup, calls zend_bailout() in php_handler that is caught by its outer zend_first_try and still runs php_apache_request_dtor -> php_request_shutdown before accepting the next request). Request N is an ordinary request that materializes superglobals (any script touching $_GET/$_SERVER), leaving PG(http_globals) dangling after shutdown. Request N+1 is shaped (large POST body buffered during sapi_activate, large/many cookies and headers, low or exhausted memory_limit) so that an allocation during request startup — before php_hash_environment runs — fails and triggers the bailout. The subsequent shutdown then double-frees the stale superglobal arrays from request N. This is the OOM-during-request-startup / per-request-state-reused-across-requests pattern echoing the circa-2004 research on PHP request-parsing (GPC) state.

findings.title: Cross-request double-free / use-after-free of the superglobal array set PG(http_globals) when request startup aborts before php_hash_environment()
findings.subsystem: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown) together with main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment) and the request-reusing SAPIs (sapi/apache2handler, sapi/cli/php_cli_server).
findings.mechanism: The six superglobal arrays ($_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES) live in the per-process core-globals array PG(http_globals)[], which is reused across every request on a long-lived worker. The ONLY place these slots are (re-)armed for a request is php_hash_environment(), which begins with memset(PG(http_globals),0,...). That function runs fairly late inside the zend_try block of php_request_startup() — after php_output_activate(), zend_activate(), and sapi_activate() (which itself reads/decodes the POST body and request headers and can allocate heavily). At the end of every request, php_request_shutdown() step 8 unconditionally loops over PG(http_globals)[] calling zval_ptr_dtor() on each slot. Crucially, after that teardown the zval slots are NOT reset to UNDEF, so once a request completes the PG(http_globals)[] entries are left as dangling IS_ARRAY zvals whose Z_COUNTED pointers reference memory that the request memory manager reclaimed at shutdown. On the NEXT request, re-arming happens only if php_hash_environment()'s memset executes. If a zend_bailout (classically triggered by hitting memory_limit during request startup — the 2004-era memory_limit interruption class — but also any early fatal/bailout) occurs after a previous request already ran but BEFORE php_hash_environment(), the memset never runs, so the dangling IS_ARRAY zvals survive into php_request_shutdown(). Step 8 then calls zval_ptr_dtor() on those stale pointers, decrementing a refcount inside freed/reused heap memory and potentially freeing it again: a use-after-free and double-free on attacker-influenceable reused heap. Note the asymmetry that makes this a real defect: shutdown steps 1, 5, and 7 are gated by `if (PG(modules_activated))` (a flag set only at the very end of php_request_startup, right after php_hash_environment), but step 8 — destroying the superglobals — has no such guard, so it runs even when the request never got far enough to initialize those arrays.
findings.reachable_how: A remote, unauthenticated HTTP client talks to a reused worker SAPI (mod_php/apache2handler or the built-in cli-server `php -S`). Both of these call php_request_shutdown() even when php_request_startup() fails/bails (apache2handler re-bails via zend_bailout inside its zend_first_try and then unconditionally runs php_apache_request_dtor->php_request_shutdown; cli-server calls php_cli_server_request_shutdown immediately on a FAILURE return). An attacker drives memory consumption toward the configured memory_limit during the early part of request startup (e.g., via request body/header processing performed in sapi_activate before php_hash_environment runs) so that an allocation fails and triggers a bailout in that window on a worker that has already served at least one prior request. The subsequent shutdown then operates on the stale PG(http_globals) pointers, yielding memory corruption that persists/recurs across the shared worker.

findings.title: Dangling/stale SG(request_info).content_type_dup pointer not cleared after free (request-startup POST handling)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c (sapi_read_post_data, sapi_handle_post, sapi_activate, sapi_deactivate_module).
findings.mechanism: content_type_dup is an estrdup'd (request-pool) string created in sapi_read_post_data(), which runs during sapi_activate() — i.e., before application code. Unlike the sibling field post_entry (which sapi_activate() always resets to NULL at request start), content_type_dup is only set to NULL on specific branches, and in sapi_deactivate_module() it is efree()'d WITHOUT being set to NULL afterward. Because it is consumed/freed-and-NULLed in sapi_handle_post() only when post_entry is non-NULL, a POST whose content-type has no registered post-entry (handled by the default reader) leaves content_type_dup set through the whole request and merely efree'd (not NULLed) at deactivate. The code at the top of sapi_read_post_data() even documents the false assumption 'content_type_dup is not set at this stage so no need to try to free it first'. If a later request reaches sapi_deactivate_module() without content_type_dup having been (re)assigned or NULLed in sapi_activate() (e.g., when SG(server_context) is not set so neither the POST nor the else-branch that NULLs it runs), the stale, already-freed pointer is efree()'d again — an invalid/double free. More generally this is a per-request SAPI-global pointer into request-pool memory that is left dangling across the request boundary rather than being reset.
findings.reachable_how: Reached during normal request setup by any remote client sending a POST with a content-type that falls through to the default post reader (so sapi_handle_post never frees content_type_dup). The dangling pointer is produced on every such request; it becomes an invalid free when a subsequent request on the same reused worker does not pass through the sapi_activate() branch that reassigns or NULLs content_type_dup before sapi_deactivate_module() frees it again.

findings.title: Cross-request use-after-free of the super-global array slots (PG(http_globals)) when request startup aborts before php_hash_environment
findings.subsystem: Request lifecycle: main/main.c (php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown) together with main/php_variables.c (php_hash_environment and the auto-global creators that populate PG(http_globals)).
findings.mechanism: PG(http_globals)[] is an array of zvals living in the persistent SAPI/per-process globals (it survives across requests on a reused worker). The arrays it points at ($_GET/$_POST/$_COOKIE/$_SERVER/$_ENV/$_FILES) are allocated from the per-request Zend memory manager. Teardown and setup are asymmetric. On teardown, php_request_shutdown step 8 unconditionally calls zval_ptr_dtor on every PG(http_globals)[i]; zval_ptr_dtor only drops the refcount and does NOT clear the source zval, so after the array (and shortly afterwards the whole request heap, via shutdown_memory_manager) is freed, each PG(http_globals)[i] still carries IS_ARRAY plus a now-dangling pointer. On setup, the ONLY place those slots are re-initialized to a clean (zeroed/UNDEF) state is the single memset(PG(http_globals),0,...) at the very top of php_hash_environment, and php_hash_environment is the LAST action inside php_request_startup's zend_try block. Therefore, if a request's startup aborts via zend_bailout anywhere before php_hash_environment runs (for example an out-of-memory / memory_limit longjmp triggered while php_output_activate, zend_activate, or sapi_activate — which reads and processes POST body, cookies and headers before any application code — is allocating), the slots are never cleared. php_request_shutdown is still invoked and its step 8 runs zval_ptr_dtor on the stale IS_ARRAY zvals left over from the PREVIOUS request. Those pointers reference memory that was already freed at the end of the prior request and very likely re-used by allocations made during the current (partial) startup, so the dtor decrements a refcount / frees an object inside recycled heap: a use-after-free / type-confusion / double-free that an attacker can influence through the contents that were placed at the recycled addresses.
findings.reachable_how: Reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker on any SAPI that keeps the worker/process alive and still calls php_request_shutdown after a failed php_request_startup. Two concrete cases in-tree: the Apache module (sapi/apache2handler/sapi_apache2.c: php_apache_request_ctor returns the php_request_startup result; on failure php_handler bails and php_apache_request_dtor -> php_request_shutdown runs, and the Apache worker thread/process continues serving further requests), and the built-in web server (sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c: php_cli_server_request_startup returning FAILURE leads to php_cli_server_request_shutdown -> php_request_shutdown while the single server process keeps accepting connections). The attacker first sends one ordinary request so the super-globals get populated and then dtor'd (leaving the dangling IS_ARRAY slots), then sends a second request crafted to make an allocation fail during early startup (e.g. under a tight memory_limit, or by inflating the pre-application allocations such as POST/cookie/header processing in sapi_activate) so the bailout happens before php_hash_environment's memset. The next php_request_shutdown then operates on the stale pointers.

findings.title: Skipped per-request RSHUTDOWN leaves extension request-parsing state uncleared on a reused worker after a startup bailout
findings.subsystem: Request lifecycle: main/main.c php_request_startup/php_request_shutdown gating on PG(modules_activated); Zend/zend_API.c zend_activate_modules; interacts with extensions that cache request-parsing arrays in module globals (e.g. ext/filter's IF_G(get_array/post_array/...)).
findings.mechanism: php_request_startup sets PG(modules_activated)=1 only AFTER zend_activate_modules (all extensions' RINIT/request_startup handlers) completes, and php_hash_environment (which, with auto_globals_jit disabled, parses GET/POST/COOKIE and lets registered input filters stash per-request arrays into module globals) runs just before that. php_request_shutdown runs the RSHUTDOWN handlers (zend_deactivate_modules) only when PG(modules_activated) is set. Consequently, if a zend_bailout (e.g. OOM) occurs during php_hash_environment or during zend_activate_modules, PG(modules_activated) stays 0 and every extension's RSHUTDOWN is skipped, even though their RINIT already ran and/or request parsing already populated module-global pointers. Those per-request pointers then dangle after the request heap is torn down. The next request on the same worker is a 'feature that runs before application code' (request parsing / input filtering) which may reuse the still-populated module-global slot instead of re-initializing it, yielding use-after-free. The code depends entirely on each extension defensively re-clearing its state in a pre-application hook (ext/filter happens to be saved only because php_sapi_filter_init, invoked from sapi_activate, resets its slots) — any extension lacking such an unconditional early reset is exposed, and the design makes RSHUTDOWN unreliable precisely in the low-memory path.
findings.reachable_how: Same reused-worker SAPIs and the same attacker model as the first finding: an unauthenticated request whose startup allocation fails (OOM/memory_limit) after RINIT handlers have run but before modules_activated is set, causing RSHUTDOWN to be skipped, followed by a subsequent request on the same Apache worker or built-in-server process that reuses the uncleared module-global request-parsing state.

findings.title: No confirmed memory-safety bug; low-confidence anomaly in Basic-auth parsing
findings.subsystem: main/main.c, php_handle_auth_data (processing of the HTTP Authorization header)
findings.mechanism: I did not confirm any remotely reachable memory-safety defect within my tool budget, so this report is a lead to check, not a confirmed root cause. The one departure from expected code I saw is here. After base64-decoding the Basic credentials, the function overwrites the first ':' with a NUL byte to split user from password. It then copies the user name with a length-bounded duplicate that uses the full decoded length, rather than a copy that stops at that NUL. The copy stays inside the decoded buffer, so I found no out-of-bounds read or write. The result is that the stored auth_user value carries the password and any later bytes behind an embedded NUL. Code that later handles PHP_AUTH_USER using the allocation length, rather than the C-string length, could expose or misuse that data. That is a logic and data-integrity problem, not proven memory corruption.

findings.subsystem: main/main.c, php_handle_auth_data (HTTP Authorization header handling, before the script runs)
findings.mechanism: Summary: I did not confirm any remotely reachable memory-safety defect. This finding is the only departure from upstream code I found, and it is a data-handling flaw, not proven memory corruption. How it works: when the Authorization header starts with 'Basic ', the rest is base64-decoded into a zend_string. The first ':' in that string is overwritten with a NUL. auth_user is then created with estrndup using the full decoded length (ZSTR_LEN of the whole string), where upstream uses estrdup, which stops at that NUL. As a result, the auth_user heap buffer holds the user name, an embedded NUL, then the full password and any other decoded bytes (which can include more NULs). The copy stays inside the source buffer's length, so I see no direct out-of-bounds read or write. The risk is to code that later treats auth_user as having a binary-safe length: it would pick up password bytes and data past the first NUL. Today PHP_AUTH_USER is registered with a strlen-based copy, which hides this. findings.title: No memory-safety defect confirmed in the request-parsing paths reviewed (audit incomplete)
findings.subsystem: Request ingestion: main/rfc1867.c (multipart/form-data parser), main/php_variables.c (GET/POST/cookie registration, argv building), main/SAPI.c (Content-Type dispatch, POST reading), main/fastcgi.c (FastCGI PARAMS parsing), ext/standard/url.c (URL decoding), ext/session (session-ID validation, files save handler path building, upload-progress callback), ext/filter (sanitizing filters and IPv4/IPv6 validation), ext/json scanner, and parts of ext/standard/var_unserializer.re.
findings.mechanism: I did not find a memory-safety root cause I can stand behind, and this audit is incomplete: I hit the tool-call budget first. This is not a clean bill of health. What I read and checked: (1) Multipart parser: the buffer is sized to max(boundary+6, 5 KB)+1, so writing the terminator at line[bufsize] stays in bounds. fill_buffer, next_line and multipart_buffer_read keep bytes_in_buffer consistent, and the read loop copies at most bytes-1 bytes. Boundaries longer than the fill unit are rejected. The lbuf used for the $_FILES names is grown with an overflow-checked reallocation before each bounded snprintf. Header continuation lines, getword and getword_conf (including escaped quotes) stay inside NUL-terminated strings. (2) Variable registration: the name is copied into its own buffer, bracket parsing modifies that copy in place, nesting depth is limited by max_input_nesting_level, and the urlencoded POST reader rescans its buffer correctly. (3) FastCGI name and value lengths are checked against the remaining record before use, and the 31-bit lengths cannot overflow when added. (4) The JSON scanner's escape accounting (5, 4, 3 and 8 bytes saved for the four \u escape forms) matches the bytes it writes when copying. (5) The session files handler checks the buffer length before building a path, and session IDs are restricted to a fixed character set and maximum length. (6) In the unserializer, back-references are bounds-checked against the used slots, string lengths are checked against the remaining input, and self-references are rejected. Areas I did not finish: the rest of the unserializer (nested array/object handling, __unserialize and __wakeup ordering), mbstring's multipart encoding-translation helpers, the FPM path-info logic I only partly compared with the CVE-2019-11043 fix, the built-in CLI web server's HTTP parser, and the per-SAPI cookie and header import code.

findings.title: Unconfirmed: the multibyte multipart header tokenizer can read past the end of the string (only with mbstring encoding_translation on)
findings.subsystem: ext/mbstring rfc1867 hooks (php_mb_rfc1867_getword / php_mb_rfc1867_substring_conf), used by main/rfc1867.c
findings.mechanism: I'm reporting this with low confidence and could not show it can actually be exploited; it appears to match upstream PHP. When encoding translation is enabled, the multipart Content-Disposition tokenizer moves forward by the byte length of each multibyte character, as reported by php_mb_mbchar_bytes. It does not check that every byte of that character is actually present before the string's NUL terminator. A lead byte of a multibyte encoding placed just before the end of a header line can make the pointer jump past the terminator. The tokenizer's loops (the main scan and the loop that skips stop characters) then keep reading heap memory past the multipart buffer line until they hit a stray NUL or the stop character. estrndup then copies a span that goes past the real line, which is an out-of-bounds read with a possible information leak. The quoted-value path in substring_conf has a matching risk: it reads one byte ahead (start[i+1]) after a trailing backslash. I could not confirm this from the bounds of the multipart buffer.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated client sends a multipart/form-data POST. PHP parses the body (rfc1867_post_handler) before any script code runs. The header-tokenizing path above only runs when mbstring.encoding_translation is enabled and a multibyte detect order or internal encoding is in effect. My review of the default code paths (multipart buffering and boundary handling, URL and form decoding, variable registration, the cookie and query-string parsers, Basic auth base64 decoding, the FastCGI record and parameter parser, FPM PATH_INFO handling, session upload progress, the JSON scanner, and the CLI server header buffering) found no confirmed memory-safety defect. All of those matched the hardened upstream logic.

findings.title: Built-in CLI web server: getallheaders()/apache_request_headers() can return a freed header value after the same header is sent twice with different letter case
findings.subsystem: sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c, request header bookkeeping (php_cli_server_client_save_header, php_cli_server_request_ctor/dtor, and the getallheaders/apache_request_headers implementation around line 419)
findings.mechanism: Each client request keeps two hash tables that point at the same persistent zend_string header values. request.headers is keyed by the lower-cased name and has a destructor (cli_header_value_dtor) that releases the value. request.headers_original_case is keyed by the name exactly as the client sent it and has no destructor, so it only borrows the pointer and never holds its own reference. When a header name arrives a second time (anything except Set-Cookie), save_header builds a new combined string "old, new" and calls zend_hash_update on request.headers. That update runs the destructor on the old value, which frees it because nothing else holds a counted reference. If the second copy used different letter case (for example "X-A" and then "x-a"), the lower-cased key matches but the original-case key does not. The update on headers_original_case therefore adds a new entry and leaves the old one untouched, still pointing at the string that was just freed. Nothing removes or refreshes that entry. Later in the same request, getallheaders()/apache_request_headers() runs zend_array_dup over headers_original_case. That copies and adds a reference to the freed zend_string, then hands it to PHP userland as an array element. This is a use-after-free of request-scoped memory that was set up during header parsing and released too early, before request teardown. Separately, in the non-Set-Cookie merge path the second incoming value string is never released, so it leaks. The root cause is a lifetime mismatch: two containers share one value, but only one of them owns it.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated network client sends a single HTTP request to a PHP built-in development server (php -S) with the same header name twice in different letter case. The bug is triggered if the router script or the requested PHP script calls getallheaders() or apache_request_headers(). This is common in frameworks that build a request object from all headers. No authentication or special configuration is needed beyond the server being reachable. The freed string's memory can be reused by later allocations before it is read, so the attacker can influence what memory the script reads or corrupts.

findings.title: Basic-auth parsing may leave auth_password stale or uninitialized (lower severity, request-state hygiene)
findings.subsystem: main/main.c php_handle_auth_data, with SAPI request_info setup and teardown in main/SAPI.c sapi_deactivate_module
findings.mechanism: For an Authorization: Basic header whose decoded text has a colon but an empty password, php_handle_auth_data sets auth_user and returns success, but never assigns SG(request_info).auth_password. The field keeps whatever value it had before this call. During normal teardown, sapi_deactivate_module frees the field and sets it to NULL, so this is usually harmless. However, the code now depends on every SAPI and every earlier path having cleared the field. A SAPI that fills in request_info without resetting auth_password, or a failed or aborted request where deactivation did not complete, would then free (in sapi_deactivate_module) or expose (in php_register_server_variables, as PHP_AUTH_PW) a stale pointer. This is a request-state setup defect: a field a remote client controls is only set on some paths.
findings.reachable_how: Any remote client can send an Authorization: Basic header that decodes to a username followed by a colon and nothing after it. Whether this causes memory corruption depends on the SAPI's request_info initialization and whether the previous request on that worker tore down cleanly.

findings.title: No confirmed defect: request setup/teardown code read so far matches upstream (unverified lead: session decode-failure path)
findings.subsystem: ext/session (session state set up and torn down within a request); also checked: main/main.c, main/SAPI.c, main/rfc1867.c, main/php_variables.c, main/output.c, main/fastcgi.c, sapi/fpm/fpm/fpm_main.c, Zend executor init/shutdown, ext/standard RINIT/RSHUTDOWN

I ran out of tool calls before I could confirm a memory-safety bug, so this entry is a pointer for follow-up, not a finding.

What I checked and found matching upstream PHP: php_request_startup and php_request_shutdown (the order of teardown steps, freeing superglobals and request globals); SAPI activate/deactivate (content_type_dup, request_body, auth fields, freeing the list of uploaded temp files); multipart upload parsing in rfc1867.c (temp file names are reference-counted correctly between the uploaded-files table and $_FILES['tmp_name'], and cleanup is correct); php_variables.c (variable registration, POST parsing, building the superglobals on first use, argv building); output layer activate/deactivate; FastCGI parameter parsing and per-request hash reset; the FPM request loop (freeing path_translated, closing the request body fd); Zend init_executor, shutdown_executor and zend_deactivate; and the standard extension's per-request init/shutdown handlers (basic, url_scanner, filestat, browscap, user_filters, assert, syslog).

The suspected bug there is ordering-related: if session data fails to decode, the code destroys the session, resets the session globals and rebuilds $_SESSION, all while the unserializer may still be in progress, and then a request-shutdown step frees the same state again. A pointer into the session array or session ID could then be used or freed twice. The pieces I did read (the session-globals reset at destroy/shutdown, php_session_track_init and the decode-failure handler) match upstream. I didn't read php_rinit_session, the session RSHUTDOWN handler, php_session_flush or the serializer callbacks, so this is unproven.
findings.reachable_how: Unconfirmed. The lifecycle code I verified runs on every request: query string, cookies, POST body, multipart uploads, FastCGI parameters and the Authorization header all go through it without authentication. I found no memory-safety defect on those paths. Whether that leads to a use-after-free or double free can't be decided without reading the session RINIT/RSHUTDOWN and flush code.

findings.title: Unconfirmed lead: request-teardown frees SAPI request strings without clearing the pointers
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module() / sapi_activate() (SAPI request lifecycle)
findings.mechanism: Low confidence; not confirmed as a bug. At request teardown, sapi_deactivate_module() frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user, but unlike auth_user, auth_password and auth_digest, it does not set either field back to NULL. Correct behaviour depends on the next request's startup overwriting both before anything reads or frees them. sapi_activate() always clears current_user. It sets content_type_dup only when a server context exists: either sapi_read_post_data() assigns it, or the non-POST path sets it to NULL. If a request starts without a server context, or startup bails out before sapi_activate() reaches that point, the field could still hold the previous request's freed pointer. Teardown would then free it a second time, or sapi_handle_post() would use it after it was freed. In the paths I could trace (the FPM and CGI loops, and the POST handlers, which clear the field after use), every request does overwrite it, and upstream PHP appears to use the same pattern, so this may not be exploitable or even a real bug. I reviewed the rest of the request lifecycle and found nothing wrong: request startup and shutdown in main.c, the executor, the output layer, superglobal creation, the cookie/GET/POST parsers, the multipart upload handler and its uploaded-files table, basic-auth decoding, FastCGI parameter parsing and per-request cleanup, and the basic extension's per-request init and shutdown. I did not get to opcache, session, the CLI built-in server, or the rest of the CGI request loop.
findings.reachable_how: Only in theory, and I did not show it. An attacker would need a persistent worker (FPM or FastCGI CGI) to tear down one request and then start the next one along a path where the server context is missing or startup aborts before the content-type field is reset. I found no unauthenticated input that forces such a path, so remote reachability is unconfirmed.

t619.why: Identifies a freed request global that is not NULLed and could be used by the next request on a reused worker, but does not involve a fatal error interrupting cleanup or a pre-application path such as session upload progress (session explicitly not reviewed).

findings.title: Stale pointers left in SAPI request info after teardown (low confidence, not a proven exploitable root cause)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c, request teardown (sapi_deactivate_module) and the following request's startup (sapi_activate)
findings.mechanism: At the end of a request, sapi_deactivate_module frees two fields of the per-request info: the lower-cased copy of the Content-Type header (content_type_dup) and the cached current-user string (current_user). Unlike the nearby fields (auth_user, auth_password, auth_digest, the status line, the mimetype), these two are not set to NULL after being freed, so they keep pointing at freed request memory across the request boundary. sapi_activate always resets current_user. It resets content_type_dup only when there is a server context: either in the POST branch or in the else branch. sapi_handle_post only uses and frees content_type_dup when a post_entry is set, and post_entry is reset to NULL at each startup. If any SAPI or error path ever skips the reset, or calls the deactivate routine twice, the stale pointer would be read or freed again: a use-after-free or double free of request memory. I believe this matches upstream PHP, and I could not confirm a path that actually reaches the stale value. Treat this as an area to harden, not a verified bug. The audit was incomplete: other code paths in the request lifecycle were not reviewed.
findings.reachable_how: In theory, any unauthenticated HTTP request with a Content-Type header, especially a POST, sets content_type_dup through sapi_read_post_data, and teardown then frees it without clearing it. Turning that into a real memory error would need a following request or error path where the per-request reset in sapi_activate does not run before the field is used. I did not find such a path in the reviewed FPM loop or in the core startup sequence.

t618.why: No allocation failure or OOM during multipart parsing is described; the finding only covers fields left unnulled after free.

t619.why: Correct subsystem: request state stale across request boundary on a reused worker. But it names a different field (content_type_dup), has no fatal-error-interrupted cleanup and no session upload progress path, and admits no reachable path.

findings.title: Unconfirmed: per-request content type copy is freed at shutdown but not cleared, which could cause a double free
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c, request startup and teardown (sapi_activate, sapi_read_post_data, sapi_handle_post, sapi_deactivate_module, sapi_activate_headers_only)
findings.mechanism: Status: not confirmed. I did not trace a concrete path that triggers this. During startup, sapi_read_post_data keeps a lowercased copy of the client's Content-Type header in SG(request_info).content_type_dup (allocated on the per-request heap). If a POST handler runs, sapi_handle_post frees the copy and sets the field to NULL. Otherwise sapi_deactivate_module frees it at the end of the request but leaves the pointer set (the same is true of current_user). The field is only reset at the start of the next request inside the server_context branch of sapi_activate: the POST-reading path sets it, the else branch nulls it. sapi_activate_headers_only, the path without a server_context, and any early exit before that branch never reset it. In any of those cases the global still points at freed memory. If that request ends normally, sapi_deactivate_module frees the stale pointer again (a double free), and anything that reads it before then reads freed memory. Because the heap is reset between requests, a stale pointer can end up pointing at a newer allocation. Freeing it would then corrupt a live object rather than crash cleanly.
findings.reachable_how: In theory, any unauthenticated HTTP request that sends a body whose Content-Type is accepted but whose handler never runs. In that case the copy is not freed early and survives until teardown. The double free would then need a later request in the same worker process (FPM, CGI or Apache module) to start without passing through the branch of sapi_activate that resets the field. Whether a normal web request can do that is the unverified step. The suggested fix is to set content_type_dup and current_user to NULL immediately after freeing them in sapi_deactivate_module.

t619.why: Identifies per-request global pointer surviving free into next request on reused worker (UAF/double free), but lacks the pre-application-code trigger like session upload progress and is unconfirmed.

findings.title: Low confidence: content_type_dup is freed at teardown but the pointer is not cleared, and startup only resets it on some paths
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c: sapi_activate, sapi_read_post_data, sapi_deactivate_module, sapi_handle_post (request state set up and torn down for POST bodies)
findings.mechanism: I did not confirm an exploitable bug. This is the most suspicious lifecycle pattern I found. SG(request_info).content_type_dup is a per-request heap string. sapi_read_post_data creates it, and sapi_handle_post frees it and sets it to NULL once the form handler has run. At teardown, sapi_deactivate_module frees it again if it is still set, but it does not set the field back to NULL. Unlike auth_user, auth_password, auth_digest and the mimetype, which are freed and nulled. The next request only resets the field inside the 'if SG(server_context)' branch of sapi_activate: either sapi_read_post_data overwrites it, or the else-branch sets it to NULL. Nothing in the request-startup path resets it otherwise; only sapi_initialize_empty_request sets it to NULL, and it also clears server_context. So the field's safety depends on every SAPI making sure that, before each request after the first, either server_context is set or sapi_initialize_empty_request has run. If a SAPI or embedder runs php_request_startup with no server context and without that reset after an earlier request that left the string unconsumed, the field still points at memory already freed by the previous request's teardown. Two things could then happen: sapi_handle_post (reached from $_POST creation or request_parse_body) passes that pointer to a body parser such as the multipart parser, which reads and writes into it while looking for the boundary, or the next teardown frees it a second time. The trigger is an unconsumed POST content type: a POST whose $_POST is never built, or one with an unrecognised content type that only goes to the default reader. I checked the CLI web server and FPM loops and could not show that either one actually reaches the bad state; the upstream code appears to have the same pattern. Treat this as a hardening gap that needs checking, not a confirmed vulnerability.
findings.reachable_how: A remote client controls the POST method, the Content-Type header and whether the script ever reads $_POST. Any long-lived SAPI that handles many requests per process (FPM, CGI/FastCGI, the CLI development server, embedders) runs this startup and teardown code on every request, so a stale pointer left by one request would be used by the next request in the same worker.

findings.title: Note: the multipart boundary is cut in place in the shared content-type copy (no defect confirmed)
findings.subsystem: main/rfc1867.c: rfc1867_post_handler working on SG(request_info).content_type_dup
findings.mechanism: The multipart handler finds the boundary inside the shared content_type_dup buffer and writes a NUL terminator into that buffer to end the boundary. The boundary length is checked against FILLUNIT, the per-part fields go through getword and getword_conf, and the counts are limited by max_multipart_body_parts, max_input_vars and max_file_uploads. I found no overflow there. I mention it because this in-place write is what would turn the stale content_type_dup in the first finding into memory corruption rather than just a stale read: the parser both reads and writes the buffer it is given.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated multipart/form-data POST to any PHP script with file_uploads or form parsing on; the parser runs during request startup or when $_POST is first accessed.

t619.why: Names per-request global state (content_type_dup) that is freed at teardown but not nulled. The stale pointer survives into a later request on a reused worker and is consumed by a pre-application path such as sapi_handle_post or the multipart parser, giving a use-after-free.

t618.why: Says nothing about an allocation failure or OOM during request startup, or about cleanup running over partially-initialized state.
