findings.title: Unconfirmed: freed per-request SAPI strings left as stale pointers, possible double free when a later request startup fails
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c request lifecycle (sapi_deactivate_module / sapi_activate / sapi_read_post_data), driven by php_request_startup and php_request_shutdown in main/main.c
findings.mechanism: Unconfirmed: not checked against upstream (it may match), and no triggering path traced end to end. At the end of a request, sapi_deactivate_module frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user but leaves both pointers set. The neighbouring auth_user, auth_password and auth_digest fields are cleared after being freed. These pointers sit in process-wide SAPI globals, so they survive into the next request on a reused worker, pointing at freed request memory. The next request's sapi_activate does not reliably reset content_type_dup first: it sets it to NULL only when there is a server context and the request is not a POST with a content type. For a POST with a content type, sapi_read_post_data only replaces the field near its end, after an earlier allocation (copying the Content-Type value). If that allocation or anything before it in php_request_startup fails, the request bails out with the stale value still in place. That includes zend_activate, which runs before sapi_activate, and failures from the memory limit or out-of-memory errors. php_request_startup catches the bailout, marks the SAPI as started and returns failure. The SAPI then runs php_request_shutdown, either directly or (in Apache's handler) via its own bailout handler. Shutdown calls sapi_deactivate_module, which frees the stale pointer a second time. That is a double free, or an invalid free, in the Zend request heap, which can corrupt the allocator's free lists. current_user has the same freed-but-not-cleared pattern on any path where startup stops before sapi_activate resets it.
findings.reachable_how: Unconfirmed. In principle, an unauthenticated remote client sends ordinary HTTP requests to a long-lived worker (Apache module, FPM or CGI/FastCGI). One request establishes a heap-allocated content_type_dup (a POST with a Content-Type), and the worker is reused. A later request then has to make request startup bail out before content_type_dup is reset, for example by hitting the memory limit or an allocation failure during startup or early POST parsing. The teardown after that failed startup frees the stale pointer again. I did not confirm that a remote request can reliably force a failure at that point.

t618.why: Describes an allocation/memory-limit failure during request startup or POST parsing that bails out, after which shutdown frees invalid (stale) request state, which is the core mechanism.

t619.why: Identifies freed SAPI globals that persist across requests on a reused worker, but the consequence it gives is a double free during failed startup, not a pre-application path such as upload progress reading the stale pointer.

findings.title: Superglobals from the previous request freed again when request startup aborts early (stale PG(http_globals))
findings.subsystem: main/main.c request startup/shutdown (php_request_startup, php_request_shutdown step 8) together with main/php_variables.c php_hash_environment
findings.mechanism: At the end of every request, step 8 of php_request_shutdown releases each entry of PG(http_globals) ($_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE, $_SERVER, $_ENV, $_FILES), but it never resets those slots to undefined. They only get cleared (with a memset) inside php_hash_environment, and that runs near the end of php_request_startup's protected block. Several things run before it in the same block and can fail by bailing out: output activation, zend_activate, sapi_activate (which reads the request body, builds a temp stream and can call the POST reader), and starting the default output buffer or handler. A memory-limit or out-of-memory error during these is the likely trigger. If one of them bails out, startup returns FAILURE before the slots are cleared, so they still point at the previous request's arrays, which were already freed and whose memory was reset by the memory manager. php_request_shutdown always runs afterwards (some SAPIs call it after any failed request setup), and it releases those stale pointers again. That is a double free / use-after-free inside the reused memory heap. The trigger is a bailout part-way through setup combined with a worker that has already served a request.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated client sends a request to a long-lived worker (Apache module, CGI in FastCGI mode, LiteSpeed, and so on) that has already served at least one request. The request is built so that startup fails before the superglobals are set up, for example by making memory run out while the POST body is read and buffered or while output buffering is started. The shutdown that follows then releases the previous request's superglobal arrays a second time.

findings.title: content_type_dup freed but not cleared at deactivation; double free if the next request aborts before sapi_activate
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c (sapi_deactivate_module / sapi_activate / sapi_read_post_data)
findings.mechanism: sapi_deactivate_module frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup (and current_user) but does not set them to NULL. The field is only reset in sapi_activate: sapi_read_post_data sets it for POST requests, or the else branch sets it to NULL. sapi_handle_post clears it correctly, but only if the post handler finishes; if the multipart or standard form handler bails out part-way, the pointer is never cleared. If the next request on the same worker bails out during php_request_startup before sapi_activate runs (for example inside zend_activate or output activation, both of which can fail under memory pressure), the request still runs SAPI deactivation and frees the same pointer a second time. This is the same root cause as the first finding: freed per-request state is not cleared and is only reset late in the next request's startup, so an error path that ends startup early tears down the previous request's leftover pointers.
findings.reachable_how: A remote client sends a POST request with a Content-Type to a reused worker, then makes a later request's startup fail early (for example through memory exhaustion). Deactivation then frees the stale content-type copy a second time.

findings.title: Freed POST content-type buffer kept as a stale global and freed again on a later request
findings.subsystem: SAPI request lifecycle (main/SAPI.c: sapi_deactivate_module, sapi_activate, sapi_read_post_data)
findings.mechanism: sapi_deactivate_module (lines 526-528) frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup but does not set it to NULL. Only some startup paths clear it again. In sapi_activate it is reset (line 475) only when there is a server context and the request is not a POST that will be parsed. For a POST, sapi_read_post_data first allocates a lowercase copy of the Content-Type with estrndup (line 174) and only stores it in content_type_dup much later (line 221). The comment there says 'not set at this stage so no need to try to free it first', but that is only true if the previous request cleared it. If the allocation at line 174 fails on the memory limit, or anything else bails out before line 221, the global still points at the previous request's freed buffer. The same happens on paths that skip the reset entirely (no server context). The next teardown sees a non-NULL content_type_dup and frees the already-freed memory again. Because the worker's heap is reused, that double free can corrupt the allocator's free lists and later hand out overlapping blocks.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated client sends ordinary HTTP POST requests to a long-lived worker such as PHP-FPM, where many requests are served by one process. The first request sets and frees content_type_dup during normal teardown. A later request on the same worker has to stop (for example a memory-limit error while copying a very long Content-Type header) before a new pointer is stored. Its teardown then frees the stale pointer a second time. I did not trace what happens before line 173 for an empty Content-Type, and I did not check SAPIs other than FPM, so how easily the early exit can be triggered is unconfirmed.

findings.title: Superglobal arrays from the previous request are freed again when request startup fails early
findings.subsystem: Request startup/shutdown (main/main.c php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown; main/php_variables.c php_hash_environment)
findings.mechanism: PG(http_globals) (the $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE, $_SERVER, $_ENV and $_FILES slots) is cleared only inside php_hash_environment (php_variables.c line 787). That runs near the end of the zend_try block in php_request_startup (main.c line 1942), after output activation, zend_activate and sapi_activate (which reads and parses the POST body). Step 8 of php_request_shutdown (main.c lines 2012-2018) releases every slot but does not reset them to undefined. If startup bails out before php_hash_environment (for example on a memory-limit or out-of-memory error during POST reading or SAPI activation), the zend_catch only records failure. The slots still hold the previous request's arrays, and the memory manager has already reclaimed them at the end of that request. The next php_request_shutdown then releases those stale values again. That decrements reference counts in freed or reused heap memory (a use-after-free / double free) inside a persistent worker.
findings.reachable_how: Remote clients reach this through normal requests to a SAPI that reuses workers. After any request has filled the superglobals, a later request that forces an early bailout during request activation (for example a large POST body that exceeds the memory limit) leaves stale superglobal pointers that are released again during shutdown. One caveat: the FPM loop I read (fpm_main.c lines 1838-1842) shuts the module down and exits when startup fails, without calling php_request_shutdown. So the exposure in FPM is narrower than this description suggests, and depends on SAPIs that continue to shutdown after a failed startup.

t619.why: It does identify per-request global state that survives after being freed on a reused worker. But the consequence it gives is a double free at teardown, not a stale read by a pre-application-code path such as session upload progress.

t618.why: An OOM/memory-limit bailout during startup (POST parsing) skips php_hash_environment, and shutdown then releases invalid, partially-initialized superglobal state.

t619.why: It identifies stale per-request globals surviving across requests on a reused worker (UAF), but the trigger is shutdown double-release, not a pre-application-code path such as session upload progress.

findings.title: SAPI request_info pointers freed at shutdown but not cleared, so they persist into the next request on a reused worker (possible use-after-free / double free)
findings.subsystem: main/SAPI.c — sapi_deactivate_module / sapi_activate / sapi_read_post_data / sapi_handle_post (request lifecycle state in SG(request_info))
findings.mechanism: Unverified lead. At request shutdown, sapi_deactivate_module frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup and SG(request_info).current_user but does not set either pointer to NULL. The fields that sit next to them (auth_user, auth_password, auth_digest) are cleared after freeing. The code relies on the next sapi_activate to reset these fields. current_user is always reset there. content_type_dup is reset only on some paths: the not-a-POST branch, the success path of sapi_read_post_data, and its fallback path for an unknown content type. A comment in sapi_read_post_data assumes the field 'is not set at this stage'. If a request bails out (for example on a memory-limit error) after the previous request's teardown but before these fields are reset, the worker keeps a dangling pointer to freed request memory. Paths that can do this include php_request_startup failing in its zend_try block, a SAPI that doesn't take the server_context path, or an allocation failure inside sapi_read_post_data before the assignment. The next shutdown would then free that pointer a second time. Or sapi_handle_post would pass the stale pointer to a post handler, such as the multipart parser, which writes into the boundary string in place. The memory manager is reset between requests and freed chunks are reused, so this would corrupt the request heap.
findings.reachable_how: An unauthenticated remote client sends requests to a persistent worker (PHP-FPM, CGI or FastCGI with request reuse, or an Apache module) that push a request into a memory-limit bailout while the request body is being set up or parsed. Examples are a large or deeply nested urlencoded or multipart POST body, or many input variables. The stale content_type_dup or current_user pointer then carries over into the worker's next request, where it is freed again or read and written. I did not confirm an exact early-bailout path, so this is a lead to check, not a proven bug.

findings.title: Superglobal arrays released at shutdown without being reset; only re-initialized late in startup
findings.subsystem: main/main.c php_request_shutdown step 8 / main/php_variables.c php_hash_environment
findings.mechanism: Unverified lead. php_request_shutdown releases each PG(http_globals) entry (the arrays behind $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE, $_SERVER and the rest) but never marks the entries as undefined afterwards. The only reset is the memset at the start of php_hash_environment, which runs late in php_request_startup. Output activation, zend_activate, sapi_activate (which reads and parses the POST body), header setup and output handler start all run before it. If startup bails out before php_hash_environment, for example on an allocation failure or memory-limit error during POST reading, the http_globals slots still hold the previous request's arrays. Those arrays were already freed, and the per-request heap was reset in between. The shutdown that follows the failed startup releases them again, which is a double free or use-after-free on the persistent worker. In FPM a failed startup ends the worker, but other SAPIs and the shutdown path itself can still reach the stale pointers. Also, the multipart parser (rfc1867) checks and fills PG(http_globals)[TRACK_VARS_FILES] during sapi_activate, which is also before the memset.
findings.reachable_how: A remote client sends a request body that drives startup into an out-of-memory or memory-limit bailout before superglobal initialization. This is likely during the POST read or multipart parse inside sapi_activate on a worker that already served a request. The teardown then operates on the previous request's freed superglobal arrays. I did not confirm this end to end.

t618.why: Describes a memory-limit/allocation failure during request startup (php_request_startup, sapi_read_post_data) that leaves request_info partially initialized. Later shutdown frees or uses that state, and multipart parsing is involved.

t619.why: Identifies a stale freed pointer carried into the next request on a reused worker (a UAF). However, it does not tie this to fatal-error-interrupted cleanup consumed by a pre-application feature such as session upload progress; it uses sapi_handle_post/content_type_dup instead.

t618.why: Describes an OOM/memory-limit bailout during startup (POST/multipart parse) before superglobal init, after which shutdown operates on invalid state.

t619.why: Identifies http_globals surviving after free into the next request on a reused worker, consumed by rfc1867 in sapi_activate before the reset, which is a pre-app-code path.

findings.title: SG(request_info).content_type_dup freed at request end but left pointing at freed memory; reused across requests and freed again if the next request's setup is cut short
findings.subsystem: SAPI request lifecycle (main/SAPI.c: sapi_deactivate_module, sapi_activate, sapi_read_post_data)
findings.mechanism: sapi_deactivate_module frees SG(request_info).content_type_dup but, unlike auth_user, auth_password and auth_digest right beside it, does not set it back to NULL. current_user has the same problem. Because SG is a per-worker global, the next request starts with a dangling pointer in that field. The field is only reset in two places: in sapi_activate when the request is not a POST (and only if a server context exists), and in sapi_read_post_data after it has already called estrndup on the Content-Type and looked up the post entry. If that allocation, or anything else before the reassignment, fails because of memory exhaustion (zend_mm_safe_error leads to a bailout), the jump unwinds past the reassignment. php_request_startup then reports failure. When the SAPI still runs request shutdown, as the Apache handler does through php_apache_request_dtor, sapi_deactivate_module frees the stale pointer a second time. That is a double free in the Zend heap, and any read of the field in between is a use-after-free. The same applies when sapi_handle_post never runs (POST variables disabled or skipped): the pointer is freed at shutdown and stays live in the global. Any SAPI or extension that checks content_type_dup for non-NULL during the next request (sapi_handle_post does) will use the freed buffer.
findings.reachable_how: A remote client sends POST requests to a long-lived worker (FPM or mod_php reuses the same process and SAPI globals for many requests). The first request leaves a freed content_type_dup behind. A later POST whose startup hits memory exhaustion before the reassignment, such as an oversized Content-Type or body handling under a low memory_limit, makes request shutdown free the stale pointer again. On Apache, request shutdown runs even when startup fails. FPM exits the process on startup failure, but it still leaves the dangling global for code that reads it.

findings.title: Superglobals destroyed at shutdown are not reset; a request whose startup aborts early destroys the previous request's arrays a second time
findings.subsystem: Main request startup/shutdown (main/main.c php_request_startup / php_request_shutdown step 8, main/php_variables.c php_hash_environment)
findings.mechanism: php_request_shutdown destroys every PG(http_globals) entry but leaves the arrays pointing at the freed (and then recycled) heap memory. The only place these slots are cleared is the memset at the start of php_hash_environment. That runs late in php_request_startup, after output activation, zend_activate, sapi_activate (POST reading) and output-handler setup. If memory exhaustion or another fatal error bails out of startup before php_hash_environment, the zend_catch only records failure. The SAPI then calls php_request_shutdown, and step 8 destroys the previous request's arrays again. The memory manager has already reset its heap, so that memory may now hold unrelated data, and the destroy decrements and frees whatever is there: a use-after-free or double free. In general, a bailout midway through startup leaves per-worker globals half-initialized, and shutdown assumes they are fully initialized.
findings.reachable_how: On a persistent worker (mod_php, which always runs request shutdown after a failed startup), an unauthenticated client causes memory exhaustion during the early startup phase. Examples: a large request body or headers processed in sapi_activate under a constrained memory_limit, or an output handler configured to start at request init. Shutdown then destroys the previous request's stale superglobals.

t618.why: Describes OOM bailout during request startup (sapi_read_post_data) that skips reassignment, after which shutdown runs over invalid state (stale content_type_dup) and double-frees it.

t619.why: Covers a request global that survives its free on a reused worker (UAF/double free), but not the session upload progress / pre-application-code consumer path.

t618.why: Names an allocation failure (memory exhaustion) that bails out of request startup and leaves state partially initialized, after which shutdown operates on that invalid state.

t619.why: Describes stale freed globals persisting across requests on a reused worker, but the consumer is the shutdown destroy path, not a pre-application feature like session upload progress.

findings.title: Superglobal slots from the previous request can be freed a second time when request startup aborts early (unconfirmed)
findings.subsystem: main/main.c request startup and shutdown, together with main/php_variables.c (where the superglobal slots are reset) and main/SAPI.c (request-body reading)
findings.mechanism: At the end of a request, shutdown step 8 releases each superglobal ($_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE, $_SERVER, $_ENV, $_FILES, $_REQUEST) with a reference-count decrement. It does not then mark the slots as empty, so they still point at those arrays. Straight afterwards the memory manager resets the request heap, which frees or reuses that memory. These pointers stay in long-lived per-process globals, so a reused worker carries them into the next request. The slots are only zeroed at the start of the superglobal setup step, which runs late in request startup. Several things run before it inside the same error-recovery block: output-layer setup, engine activation, SAPI activation (which reads and buffers the POST body and reads cookies), the timeout setup, the version header, and starting any configured output handler. Any of these can hit a fatal error and jump straight to the error handler. Running out of the memory limit or out of system memory does exactly this, because the allocator's error path ends in that jump. If it happens, startup returns failure while the slots still point into the previous request's freed heap. When the host then runs request shutdown, step 8 runs regardless of whether startup finished and decrements counters inside freed or reused memory. Because the slots are also left unchanged by this second shutdown, the same pointers can be released again on the request after that. The result is a use-after-free or double free in the request heap.
findings.reachable_how: A remote client controls the request body, cookies and query string, which are read during SAPI activation, before the superglobals are reset. If the client can make that early stage fail with a fatal error (for example by exhausting the memory limit or system memory while the body is buffered), it aborts before the reset. This matters most on long-lived workers that serve many requests and that still run request shutdown after a failed startup, for example web-server-embedded PHP. Not confirmed: in FPM a failed startup makes the worker exit without running shutdown, so the crash path does not apply there. I did not check whether the Apache module or the CGI/FastCGI loop runs shutdown after a failed startup.

t618.why: Describes a memory exhaustion fatal during request startup that aborts before the superglobals are reset, after which shutdown operates on the invalid stale slots. This matches OOM during setup followed by cleanup over invalid state.

t619.why: Identifies stale per-request global pointers that survive the free and reach the next request on a reused worker, leading to a use-after-free. It ties this to startup OOM, though, not to a fatal error interrupting cleanup, and it never names the pre-application consumer (session upload progress).
